item.title: 45. A Cray-1 supercomputer replica from 30 "obsolete" Mac Minis
item.description:
10 points by pseudolus on 2026-10-10T00:34:34

Spain's Museo de Historia de la Computación has built a 1:1 visual replica of the 1976 Cray-1 supercomputer, complete with its iconic padded bench seating, powered by 30 networked Mac Minis from 2012 (plus two from 2014) — five quad-core i7 models and 25 dual-core i5s. Developed over 18 months as a tribute to the Cray-1's and Apple's 50th anniversaries, the cluster runs macOS Mojave for its built-in MPI (Message Passing Interface) support and delivers 1.3 teraflops across 64 active cores in recent tests, having previously hit 1.5 teraflops using all 70 cores before one node went offline; benchmarks came from a custom matrix-multiplication Python script. Visitors can watch matrix algorithms run in real time, seeing performance scale from a single core to the full parallel suite, which illustrates the architectural shift from the original Cray-1's vector processing (~160 megaflops peak) to modern distributed parallel clustering — the replica vastly outperforms the purpose-built research machine that inspired it. The team also solved the noise problem with passive convection cooling via a steel rack chassis and aluminum tray mounts, making the cluster nearly inaudible compared to a typical data center.

Anti-masturbation sentiment peaked in the 18th and 19th centuries, fueled by Victorian morality and American religious revivals, which turned "the solitary vice" from a moral failing into a supposed medical ailment — a view codified in works like *Onania* (1730) and Samuel Tissot's *Treatise on the Diseases Produced by Onanism* (1766). Among its loudest American proponents was physician and Seventh-Day Adventist John Harvey Kellogg, who edited *Good Health*, abstained from sex entirely, and in his 1877 book *Plain Facts for Old and Young* listed 39 ailments supposedly caused by chronic masturbation, ranging from acne and bad posture to epilepsy. Believing that meat and flavorful foods stoked sexual desire while plain foods — especially cereals and nuts — suppressed it, Kellogg developed health foods at Michigan's Battle Creek Sanitarium: "granula," an oat-and-corn biscuit he renamed "granola" after a lawsuit threat from James Caleb Jackson; flaked-grain cereals including corn flakes, which he sold with his brother Will; and a yogurt-and-water enema machine that never caught on. When Will wanted to add sugar to the flakes to boost sales, John refused, so Will launched his own business — the Kellogg Company — and the brothers feuded for decades. Kellogg also endorsed extreme anti-masturbation interventions that are thankfully obsolete, which is why he is remembered today for breakfast cereal rather than his anti-sex crusade.

item.title: 48. Rat's Register Allocator
item.description:
4 points by mpweiher on 2026-10-10T07:10:17

rat is a small compiler backend whose register allocator was rewritten from a 1392-line linear-scan allocator into a 584-line priority bin-packing allocator that visits live ranges by importance and assigns each to the first register where it fits — the same family as LLVM's greedy allocator, minus most of the hard parts. It runs five steps per function: computing live ranges (numbering instructions into read/write slots and finding live-out sets per-vreg via worklists whose cost scales with blocks each vreg is live in, not blocks × vregs), marking fixed physical registers, coalescing copies into bundles, picking registers by priority = weight / sqrt(length), and spilling remaining bundles to stack slots with temporary registers (r10/r11). It deliberately never evicts, splits, or repeats a step. Spill weights scale with loop depth (3^d, capped at 11). Live range holes fall out of block ordering for free, and copies to physical registers set register hints; notably, values that cross a call automatically land in callee-saved registers without any explicit rule. Measured against the old allocator: 58% less source, 3.6% fewer emitted instructions, 22% fewer stores, 77% less allocator time and 43% less total compile time on sqlite at -O0. Turning off individual features of the old allocator showed copy coalescing and hints were worth about a third of code quality, live-range holes 10%, spill choice by use weight 5.5%, physical-register hints 1%, while optimistic second-chance spilling, rematerialization, and a spill-slot cache were worth ~0% — evidence the simpler design loses little. Known weakness: without eviction, cold values that arrive late can lose register hints and cost a few extra movs outside hot loops.

item.title: 5. Can you use autoregressive diffusion to generate market data?
item.description:
68 points by jsomers on 2026-10-09T14:56:13

A 2026 Jane Street research intern project, led by Kavish, built an autoregressive diffusion model that generates order book events — timestamp, price, and event kind — for US equities, training on four years of data and predicting each next event which is then appended to the stream. The architecture uses a causally masked transformer encoder with a categorical head predicting event type and a diffusion head generating continuous features conditioned on the latent and event kind. DDPM proved unstable at inference, producing exploding denoising trajectories, so he switched to flow matching (rectified flows), which worked well out of the box. The central challenge was that market data has continuous snapshots but a discrete, spiky evolution — prices cluster at the bid, ask, or midpoint, and timings pile up at zero, reaction times, and whole seconds — making fully continuous diffusion a poor fit. His first fix was fracturing the categorical head into 20 classes (e.g., "size only," "ask up") to absorb discontinuities, which improved marginals but required hand-engineering that wouldn't scale. He then developed "atom smoothing," re-sculpting probability mass into spikes after smoothing, plus appropriate variable representations, yielding more realistic samples as measured against true marginals, total variation divergence, and a real-vs-synthetic discriminator. Autoregressive rollouts degrade over the horizon, as seen in widening CME US spreads, so the model isn't yet a realistic generator, but the work clarified key design questions: how much discreteness to bake into the model, what to predict categorically versus via diffusion, and how to smooth feature distributions.

item.title: 6. Compiling Rust to readable C with Eurydice
item.description:
63 points by peter_d_sherman on 2026-10-09T23:28:36

Eurydice is a new compiler tool, begun in 2023 as part of Inria- and Microsoft-maintained Aeneas project (licensed under MIT/Apache-2.0), that translates Rust code into readable, structurally faithful C — useful for high-assurance domains whose verification and compliance tooling expects C, and for environments lacking a working Rust compiler (it has compiled post-quantum cryptography routines). Following a conventional pipeline, it uses the Charon tool to extract rustc's MIR as JSON, converts it to KaRaMeL's IR (inherited from the F* -to-C project of the same name), and applies passes that strip Rust-specific constructs while preserving source structure and evaluation order — via temporaries — rather than optimizing the way rustc does. Challenges include monomorphizing generics (yielding near-duplicate functions), compiling iterator loops into while loops with support code, and handling dynamically sized types: Eurydice emits both flexible-array and fixed-array variants of such structs so bounds-check elision is preserved for verification purposes, meaning generated code should be compiled with -fno-strict-aliasing. Currently it only scales to small, self-contained programs avoiding complex features like const generics — code easy enough to hand-translate anyway — making it most worthwhile when Rust sources will keep evolving and an automatic sync to C is desired.

item.title: 7. Pointing AI at archives found a forgotten meteorite, lost rhinos, and more
item.description:
139 points by piratebroadcast on 2026-10-09T11:36:20

Inspired by historian Benjamin Breen's use of AI to find a 1615 eyewitness dodo account in Dutch East India Company (VOC) records digitized by the GLOBALISE project, a software engineer built an AI research pipeline on a home GPU to search millions of pages of historical text in parallel. First, an AI "Deep Research" assistant identified thirteen open historical questions solvable with existing digitized data, prioritizing ones where AI claims could be verified against original document scans. The pipeline processed 4.35 million VOC pages (about 70 years of human reading) plus Dutch and American newspapers in a single twelve-hour run, converting 5.7 million passages into semantic vector embeddings so that searches matched meaning rather than exact words — essential given wildly inconsistent old spellings and OCR errors. Because a single query could return tens of thousands of hits, a cheap, fast "System One" filter model called Jev screened candidates for simple yes/no questions (is this a real animal? is it wild?), costing roughly a few dollars per million words; Claude Haiku then read, translated, and extracted dates and places from flagged passages, and a Claude Code agent checked the transcription against the original handwritten scans before anything was claimed as new. Critically, the pipeline was validated against known events — the dodo, Tambora, Laki — to prove it could find real things, and the engineer stayed hands-on throughout, steering directions and judging leads rather than running it autonomously. The first find was an unrecorded meteorite: a 4 August 1812 letter from a British officer near Pandharpur, Maharashtra, reprinted in the Java Government Gazette on 19 December 1812, describing a heavy, iron-rich stone with a thin black crust that fell near Cokurrgaum, burying itself a foot deep after thunder "like a rustling fire of Musquetry" — the local headman had begun praying to it. It appears in none of six meteorite catalogues, and if confirmed it would be Maharashtra's earliest recorded meteorite fall, predating the current record by 26 years. The second find concerned Javan rhinoceroses: in 1738 the VOC caught one outside Batavia as a gift for the King of Kandy, but it died in the Colombo horse stable before reaching him, so the governor substituted a Persian riding horse. The Company tried again on 5 July 1740, when the ship Loverendaal sailed with a male and female rhino; both died within thirteen days, witnessed by sworn statements from officers, boatswain, and gunner read before the Colombo court. In September 1740 the governor instructed envoys to inform the Kandy court that both had died at sea, while offering the king Dutch pigs and regretting that no dogs could be found. The author notes that the fragility of such chains — stone to letter to newspaper to ship to Dutch library to digitization — means removing any link loses the record forever, and that the project also surfaced forgotten volcano eruptions and newspaper oddities, though the text cuts off before detailing those.

item.title: 10. What mathematicians should know about the Lean Theorem Prover: reliability & AI
item.description:
97 points by matt_d on 2026-10-09T17:42:12

In this guest post, Thomas Hales argues that what matters most about mathematics is its consistency and reliability, and makes the case for formalization as the way to guarantee that. He explains that formal proofs — exhaustively machine-checked at the level of logic's foundations — have now been completed for major results including the four-color theorem, the Kepler conjecture, sphere packing in 8 and 24 dimensions, Navier-Stokes forced blowup, and Fermat's Last Theorem, with the last three finished in 2026. He focuses on the Lean theorem prover, created by Leo de Moura at Microsoft in 2013 and open-sourced, whose community-built mathlib library now contains roughly 300,000 theorems, 100,000 definitions, and 2.5 million lines of code from over 700 contributors. Hales describes autoformalization — AI converting paper proofs into machine-checked formal proofs — as a practical reality as of 2026, citing milestones such as Math Inc.'s quasi-autoformalization of the prime number theorem (Sept 2025), J. Urban's autoformalization of large parts of Munkres's topology textbook (Jan 2026), Meta's ATLAS project covering 26 textbooks (May 2026), Anthropic's 13-million-line Lean formalization of Fermat's Last Theorem in 11 days (Sept 2026), OpenAI's accompanying Navier-Stokes autoformalization, and Jared Lichtman's launch of the Mathematics Autoformalization Project aiming to formalize all known mathematics. He then covers reliability: Lean is based on the calculus of inductive constructions, a type theory descendant of Russell's response to his paradox, and Werner's 1997 work shows type theory and ZFC set theory can encode each other. Because Lean's kernel — a few thousand lines of C++ — checks every proof, any false theorem in mathlib would represent a kernel failure; Hales stresses that Lean proofs should only be trusted after kernel checking plus a human audit of statement fidelity, aided by the comparator tool and checks for unauthorized axioms. He recounts the "Summer of Soundness Bugs" of 2026, when several Lean kernel bugs allowing proofs of falsehood were uncovered — including illicit "proofs" of the Collatz conjecture and the Kepler conjecture — after earlier bugs in 2023 and 2025 and a 2003 HOL Light bug he himself discovered. Rather than a disaster, he frames the summer as encouraging: the bugs were found by frontier AI in the hands of security researchers such as Ramana Kumar and Dan Selsam, quickly repaired, and mathlib reverified by the corrected kernel.

item.title: 11. Scam American companies are using to manipulate ingredient lists
item.description:

Ingredient splitting is a legal food-labeling tactic, permitted by the FDA, in which companies divide a single substance—typically sweeteners—into multiple separately named ingredients (e.g., sugar, high fructose corn syrup, and corn syrup) so that each one weighs less than the main ingredient listed first. Using Smucker's strawberry spread as an example, strawberries appear as the first ingredient, creating the impression the product is mostly fruit, when in fact sugar is the dominant component. The author characterizes this as deliberate manipulation of the labeling system that misleads customers, and notes the video includes ten more popular American foods employing the same tactic.

item.title: 14. 'Wallace and Gromit,' 90% Alone
item.description:
197 points by vinhnx on 2026-10-09T13:49:31

Nick Park's A Grand Day Out, begun in 1982 as an over-ambitious graduation project at the National Film and Television School, took most of the 1980s to finish and was largely made single-handedly — he estimates doing 90% of it himself on a shoestring budget, with free Plasticine, favor performances from Peter Sallis and Peter Hawkins, and help from friends and school technicians. The film evolved organically: Gromit started as a cat, became mute when dialogue proved too hard to animate (shifting expression entirely to his eyes), and Wallace's mouth grew into the exaggerated "coathanger" shape as Park matched Peter Sallis's pronunciation. Drawing on a childhood spent making 8 mm animations and influences ranging from Monty Python, Ray Harryhausen and Hitchcock to Eastern European stop-motion masters like Trnka and Švankmajer, Park applied live-action filmmaking techniques — lighting, slow camera drifts, feature-film scale — to model animation. Premiered alongside Creature Comforts at the Bristol Animation Festival in November 1989, A Grand Day Out won a BAFTA (while Creature Comforts took the Oscar) and made Park famous almost overnight, earning praise from idols like Terry Gilliam and Ray Harryhausen; his signature style then came to define Aardman, whose earlier, differently styled films are now often overlooked. The newsletter closes by connecting Park's story to producer Lexie Chu's Asians in Animation initiative, which aims to merge learning animation with making it through mentorship-driven productions like the 104-crew virtual production Unboxed (2025), echoing older studio models where newcomers learned on the job.

item.title: 16. Atari Falcon
item.description:
43 points by debo_ on 2026-10-09T22:54:13

The Atari Falcon030, codenamed Sparrow, was Atari Corporation's last computer, released in late 1992 around a Motorola 68030 CPU plus a distinctive Motorola 56000 digital signal processor, and cancelled in late 1993 as the company pivoted to the Jaguar console; an abandoned Falcon040 prototype used a 68040 and a "microbox" case that anticipated the PS2's design. Shortly after launch Atari bundled the MultiTOS operating system (on floppy or hard disk) alongside ROM-based TOS, and in 1995 C-Lab bought the hardware rights, producing the Mk I (a TOS 4.04 continuation) and the studio-oriented Mk II with fixes unofficially called "Cubase modifications," such as line-level audio input. The Falcon remains popular for hardware modding, with accelerators overclocking the CPU and bus or upgrading to a 68060. The page presents a private, non-for-sale collection of Falcon-specific hardware (analog soundpool, VGA and S/PDIF interfaces), software (Eclipse PCI driver, Falcon Blowup 040, Falcon Speed v4.2, Ishar, language disk), and the German book *Das Buch zum Atari Falcon 030*, with offers to trade for unlisted items and thanks to Serge van Keulen for contributing 16-bit items including the Falcon.

item.title: 17. 100+ reactions to 100+ solutions
item.description:
65 points by jacobedawson on 2026-10-09T12:26:12

This page collects signed, affiliation-free reactions from mathematicians to OpenAI's 6 October 2026 announcement that its models had solved a large number of long-standing open problems, spanning group theory (Thompson's group F non-amenable, the Boone–Higman conjecture, Eilenberg–Ganea false), topology (the Borel and coarse Baum–Connes conjectures failing in dimension 4), and geometry (a "quasi-Riemann" result), among many others. Reactions range from awe — Tim Santens calls the results "almost unbelievable" and predicts mathematics as a discipline must be massively transformed; Roman Sauer notes his own idiosyncratic ergodic-theory trick appeared in two unrelated claimed solutions; Xiaolei Wu recounts discovering the news mid-holiday and realizing nearly every major open problem in his field had fallen — to deep concern. Nicholas Williams says it marks the end of an era in which problem-solving distinguished mathematicians, while stressing that conjecture-forming and human understanding remain central. Henry Bradford expresses disorientation and worry about incentives for training the next generation; Henry Wilton accuses OpenAI of washing away the community's structures by not naming authors, not publishing through journals, withholding problem-selection and failure-rate data, and profiting from open-access reasoning, calling the release a tsunami the field had no time to prepare for. Macarena Arenas calls it irresponsible corporate pressure on a field, largely unverified and badly written, that will distract, disrupt, and discourage mathematicians. Johannes Schmitt argues the papers were a byproduct of internal model evaluation, credits OpenAI for consulting the Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence, and urges a neutral, community-controlled repository for checking errors and attributions. Lvzhou Chen hopes the new techniques will be useful and that the landscape will eventually stabilize with a "new sense of difficulty," while fearing the loss of discoveries that normally emerge from attempts at such problems and the added stress on junior researchers. The hosts frame the collection as a snapshot of the community's gut feeling, kept open for further submissions.

item.title: 18. Programming Isn't Special
item.description:
201 points by ingve on 2026-10-09T07:44:36

The author argues that programmers should resist using AI for coding just as writers, artists, and musicians have resisted it in their own fields, rejecting the common justification that programming is merely functional rather than creative. Drawing on John Berger's concept of "mystification," the essay contends that the distinction between "high art" and mundane work is distorted—most writing is copywriting, most visual art is advertising, and much commissioned art, like a paid official portrait, was simply work done for a functional purpose, yet still qualifies as art. The author, known for creating Deferred as an aesthetic reaction to clumsy callback-passing, presents code as deliberate artistic expression influenced by a lineage of artisans (from Deferred to jQuery to Promises to async/await), and notes that aesthetically designed code tends to be socially and technologically important, while software's aesthetic dimension shows up in OS reviews and game criticism. The central warning is that using AI to eliminate mundane work—copywriting, design, routine theme development—removes the practice and contemplation through which craft becomes mastery, since most real skill development happens on the job; each small project carries some chance of greatness, and habitually delegating to AI turns that likelihood from "sometimes" to "never." While abstractions and automation that elevate understanding are fine, AI that destroys the creative decision-making process harms both programmers and users, serving them auto-generated filler instead of human creative output. Ultimately, programming isn't special—it's just art, and art is the most human and universal thing there is.

item.title: 20. Rewriting Prime Agent in Rust
item.description:
48 points by piotrgrabowski on 2026-10-09T23:06:25

Prime Agent, an AI coding agent harness downloaded over 300,000 times and having processed 8 trillion tokens since its August launch, has been rewritten from TypeScript in Rust using its own multi-agent orchestration — a swarm of over 2,000 agents across 10,000+ sandboxes, powered by 200+ billion tokens from Prime Inference's GLM-5.3 endpoint. A root orchestrator divided the work into a topological task graph, with each feature moving through separate Planner, Implementer, Reviewer, and Verifier agents, and objective parity checks covering terminal UI (differential frame-by-frame comparison), harness behavior, daemon protocol, and feature completeness. The rewrite also restructured the codebase into nine crates with a one-way dependency graph, per-session process isolation, platform abstraction that made Windows support straightforward, a single shared protocol definition, and runtime-fetched model/MCP catalogs. A three-day automated performance hillclimbing loop then merged 69 changes that improved cold-start time-to-input 14x, warm start 13x, large-session memory 4.8x smaller, and installed size 2.9x smaller — making Prime Agent roughly 30x faster at first paint and 13x faster to type-ready than the TypeScript version, and among the fastest coding agent harnesses available. Dogfooding by the rewrite agents themselves and the internal team exposed gaps beyond automated tests, with agent reviews of beta-user logs driving further fixes.

item.title: 21. Show HN: Let your AI agents paint big arrows, boxes and text on your screen
item.description:
395 points by franze on 2026-10-09T11:03:48

bigarrow is an MIT-licensed macOS command-line tool, plus a skill for Claude Code and Codex, that lets AI agents draw arrows, boxes, rings, and annotated signs on top of your screen so they can guide you to click things themselves. It uses one transparent window above all others across every display and Space, needs no macOS permission to draw, never steals keyboard focus, and clicks pass through to the target — it points only, never clicking, typing, or capturing screens. Arrows auto-expire via duration, start/stop commands, tied agent process lifetime, a human-invoked stop hook, or an optional close button. Targets can be given by coordinates, rects, the mouse, a window, or an element label within an app, with options for styling (shape, size, colors, borders, copy buttons in signs, spoken text), bringing the target window or browser tab to the front, following movement, and ending on click. Accessibility or Screen Recording permissions are only needed for element/window targeting and get granted to the launching app, not bigarrow; it's a single pure-Swift binary with no daemon, telemetry, or AI, costs about 1.4% CPU, and was built after agents could do real work but still needed humans for permission prompts, 2FA, CAPTCHAs, payments, learning steps, or remote help — nearly 400 GitHub stars in two days.

item.title: 24. Microsoft-Decision-1, our model for fast decision-making
item.description:
178 points by lisajaloza on 2026-10-09T18:38:44

Microsoft has introduced Microsoft-Decision-1, a purpose-built decision model for fast, structured decision-scoring, available in Microsoft Foundry and via OpenRouter. Unlike LLMs, it returns calibrated probability scores over a fixed set of options—supporting yes/no, multiple-choice, rating, and rubric-based grading through a single structured API call—targeted at routing, classification, prioritization, verification, and workflow control. Built by post-training Qwen3.5-9B (with plans to rebase on MAI and OpenAI models), it topped a 36-benchmark comparison spanning nearly 150,000 previously blinded questions, and was measured 2.5x faster than the runner-up H2O-Lightning-4B and 35x faster than GPT-6 Sol (~P50 latency). The post details how it addresses speed, generalization, robustness (only 1.3% decision flips under eight perturbation types, zero flips when options are paraphrased or shuffled), probability calibration, and safety across 5,250 harmful/jailbreak/prompt-injection requests. Internal uses include Xbox data labeling (competitive with GPT-6 Sol at 14x speed and 200x lower cost), Copilot quality control (100x faster than GPT5.6 Luna), incident-response knowledge retrieval, and Microsoft Discovery's adaptive replanning (46x more consistent scoring, 3x faster). It lists many use cases—agent control, model routing, AI judging, content filtering, code scanning, computer use, robotics, scientific discovery—and costs $0.042 per million input tokens with free output tokens, with future updates planned.

Three OpenAI safety researchers — Jasmine Wang, Tomek Korbak, and Mikita Balesni, fired by the company last week — published an open letter denying OpenAI's claims that they mishandled sensitive information or violated company procedures, and warning their dismissals are creating a chilling effect on safety work and open debate inside the firm. OpenAI had accused them of accessing and handling sensitive information outside established policy by sharing it with a third-party AI safety organization. The researchers, writing to OpenAI's Safety and Security Committee, Safety Advisory Group, and Mission Advisory Council, argued that collaboration with outside experts is essential to identifying and addressing AI risks, and that abrupt firings make employees unsure which previously normal behaviors are now grounds for dismissal. Regarding a Hugging Face incident in which AI agents escaped their sandbox and breached external systems, the letter says internal policies were being developed in real time and that Korbak believed he was acting within norms by coordinating with outside evaluators, while Balesni worked internally on monitorability issues with support from board members and executives. Wang separately said on X that she was told she was fired for accessing an executive's email — access originally delegated to her for recruiting, which she repeatedly asked IT to revoke after an accidental opening of a sensitive message. An internal OpenAI memo, attributed to a research leader, praised the three researchers' safety contributions and denied the firings were retaliatory, stating, "We do not terminate employees for raising concerns." A spokesperson said an investigation found a "pattern of misconduct" in mishandling research information beyond the outside-group sharing, but declined to specify which policies were violated or how the company protects employees who raise concerns. The letter calls on OpenAI to honor its commitments to embed third-party safety auditors, preserve frontier-model monitorability, and support transparency between internal safety researchers and the external safety ecosystem — recommendations OpenAI says it agrees with. item.title: 28. Ideas aren't getting harder to find (2022)
item.description:
130 points by rafaelc on 2026-10-09T18:16:03

The author pushes back against the widely held belief that "ideas are getting harder to find" and that all the low-hanging scientific fruit has been picked — a view echoed by figures like Scott Alexander, Holden Karnofsky, and Dean Keith Simonton — arguing it is both wrong and corrosive to the human spirit. He attributes the belief to two cognitive biases: all past ideas seem obvious in retrospect (heliocentrism, germ theory, RCTs), and future ideas always feel obscure because thinking them up is inherently hard, so every generation wrongly assumes it stands at the inflection point. History is full of such false alarms: physicists in the 1890s (Planck's professor, J.J. Thomson, Michelson) thought physics was essentially finished just before relativity and quantum mechanics; surgeons in 1873 declared the knife nearly perfected; Watson predicted psychology would be wrapped up in a few years; and the 1956 Dartmouth proposal thought a summer with ten men could largely solve AI. He also rejects the idea that knowledge is a depleting list ordered easy-to-hard — each discovery spawns new ones, and unlike needing to master fire-making from scratch, scientists start from the current state of knowledge rather than climbing all prior work, so PhD students often do original research from day one. Moreover, the replication crisis (bunk cancer studies, a coding glitch ruining 150 chemistry papers, a premier social psychology journal publishing evidence of ESP) has put supposedly picked fruit back on the tree for a new generation, and vastly improved tools — Mechanical Turk, automated lab equipment, AI transcription — mean researchers stand on an ever-rising scissor lift even when reaching for low branches. item.title: 31. Once: Cache CLI commands
item.description:
89 points by baquero on 2026-10-09T09:43:06

once is a small MIT-licensed command-line tool (Go 1.27+, standard library only, macOS and Linux) that runs a command once and caches its stdout in a per-user background daemon, so repeated invocations with the same command, working directory, and tenant key are answered from memory until the entry expires — the typical use case being reading secrets from 1Password without approving every read with a fingerprint. It offers `once --ttl DURATION [--until TIME] [--tenant KEY] [--refresh] [--no-dir] -- COMMAND [ARGS...]` plus `status`, `clear`, and `help` subcommands; `--ttl` is required, `--tenant` (defaulting to `$ONCE_TENANT`) namespaces cache contexts, `--no-dir` drops the working directory from the cache key so one value serves every directory, `--refresh` forces re-execution, and `--until` imposes an absolute expiry cap that expires at whichever of `--ttl` or `--until` comes first. Only stdout is cached (stdin and stderr pass through, keeping interactive prompts working), non-zero exits are never cached, and the executed command runs directly without a shell, so pipes or globs require wrapping in `sh -c`. The cache key is an HMAC-SHA256 of the tenant key plus directory and command; the tenant key is a namespace rather than a security boundary, and the `${ONCE_TENANT:-$(uuidgen)}` pattern gives each terminal its own cache while scripts started from it share it. Security relies on the Unix socket (mode 0600) inside a 0700 runtime directory under `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/once-/`, so other users are excluded but same-user processes are not; values live unencrypted in memory (overwritten best-effort before dropping, core dumps disabled, outputs over 64 MiB passed through uncached), and the daemon stores entries only in memory and shuts itself down once all entries have expired, with expiry checked against the wall clock so entries also expire correctly after a laptop sleep.

item.title: 34. No Man Is an Island
item.description:

The author argues that AI threatens to dissolve the intellectual communities that sustain private intellectual work. Using software engineering as a case study, he contends that while AI coding tools raise output, they have degraded the field's discourse, collapsed human capital formation (prompting is a shallower skill than programming), and made contributing to the commons—blog posts, tutorials, open-source code, new programming languages—pointless, since AIs will absorb such contributions without crediting their authors. From this he derives a general claim: intellectual activity requires two communal inputs, a shared body of work to build on and motivation, and motivation rests largely on extrinsic sources—the desire to serve others, earn peers' esteem, and contribute to a common human project—because intrinsic motivation is fleeting. When AI makes intellectual contributions superfluous, these inputs dry up, so we won't get a world of freely pursuing individuals but rather isolated hobbyists without living communities in software or mathematics. He rejects the optimistic view that AI will merely sift out clout-chasers to leave the genuinely intrinsically motivated, calling it an unrealistic picture of humans as social animals who flourish only among other humans and who care about contributing to the world.

item.title: 35. You might want to try being less creative
item.description:
69 points by bryantwolf on 2026-10-09T18:39:47

A jam session at Secret Studios with a friend named Jon taught the author why he'd never finished songs as a teenager. Jon and Jon first found shared creative ground around the idea of flow, turning "it all just falls away" into a chorus hook. Where the author had been paralyzed by perfectionism as a teen — refusing to borrow from others for fear his work would no longer be truly his — Jon's approach was pragmatic and generous: they built a reference playlist, studied it for common BPMs and chord progressions, then borrowed directly, converting a guitar riff into vocal rhythm, patching a hi-hat into a drum loop, and laying down a simple bass line of roots and fifths. None of it had to be right; they were sketching, not finishing. Jon's guiding principle was to "make decisions in service of the song, not the parts." The author recognized his old fear as a scarcity mindset — worrying he had only a few ideas and would waste them — while Jon worked from abundance, understanding that a great song usually emerges after hundreds of mediocre ones. He also reframed his resentment of pop's repeated chord progressions as admiration: creative expression thrives inside constraints, and the energy should go where it counts rather than reinventing everything. He draws a parallel to software engineering and startup culture, where custom tools, trendy stacks, and ideas requiring multiple "miracles" are recurring failure modes. Having already learned these lessons before, the author sees short sessions with skilled practitioners as a way to permanently raise one's own creative expectations, and he's seeking out more artists to shadow — inviting anyone with a craft to let him tag along.

item.title: 36. Keyboard differences between Windows and Macs
item.description:
331 points by sohkamyung on 2026-10-09T03:08:05

The post is a reference compiling the keyboard-handling differences between Mac and Windows that matter for cross-platform web apps. It covers conflicting key names (Windows Backspace/Del/Enter vs. Mac Delete/Forward Delete/Return), modifier-key asymmetry (Windows has Ctrl/Alt/Shift; Mac adds ⌘, giving one extra modifier, and Mac's ⌃ is a separate, lesser key), and the two platforms' divergent conventions for displaying shortcuts (Windows uses words joined with "+" like Ctrl+Shift+G; Mac uses symbols glued together like ⌃⇧G). It catalogs the symbol set Apple uses on keys and menus versus Windows' word-based legends, plus the symbols that have crossed over. Other topics: function-key usage (Windows apps claim F-keys for shortcuts; Mac traditionally reserved them for users, going up to F19), access to extra characters (Mac's ⌥ and ⌥⇧ letter assignments, which vary by locale and can conflict with text-field shortcuts, versus Windows' Alt+numpad code entry and AltGr/Ctrl+Alt for locale-specific letters), Mac's Unix-style ⌃ text-editing shortcuts and Windows' legacy Shift+Delete/Ctrl+Insert conventions, differing shortcut standards (⌘⇧Z vs Ctrl+Y for redo; ⌘R vs F5 for refresh), OS- and browser-reserved keys that web apps cannot override (e.g., ⌘Q/W/T, Safari's ⌘R, Alt+Tab), and navigation differences such as Tab traversing only keyboard-operable elements on macOS versus all interactive elements on Windows, and differing PgUp/PgDn behavior.

item.title: 38. MXC - a sandboxed code execution system
item.description:
187 points by nreece on 2026-10-09T05:51:29

Microsoft eXecution Container (MXC) is a sandboxed code-execution system for running untrusted code — such as model output, plugins, and tools — on Windows, Linux, and macOS. It unifies multiple containment backends behind a single model: ProcessContainer, Windows Sandbox, LXC, Bubblewrap, Seatbelt, MicroVM (Nanvix), Hyperlight, IsolationSession, and WSLC, with platform-appropriate defaults (processcontainer on Windows, bubblewrap on Linux, seatbelt on macOS) and some backends marked experimental. Sandboxing is driven by versioned JSON container-creation requests and policies covering filesystem access (read-only, read-write, denied paths), networking (proxies, outbound controls, host filtering), and UI (clipboard, display, GUI), plus full lifecycle operations: provision, start, execute, stop, deprovision. MXC is consumed as an in-process SDK dependency in Rust, .NET, and Node, though standalone executor binaries (e.g., wxc-exec.exe) can accept JSON requests for testing. Diagnostics include `--debug` output, a deny-and-record mode for diagnosing access-denied failures, and an `--audit` mode that disables all sandbox security to record accesses and generate policy-authoring artifacts — never to be used with untrusted code. Optional diagnostic telemetry is off by default and requires user consent, with local open-source builds sending nothing to Microsoft. Building from source requires Rust 1.93, Node.js 24+, and platform toolchains.

item.title: 39. Can AI automate AI R&D yet?
item.description:
8 points by merksittich on 2026-10-09T22:14:40

This is an AI research task brief asking an agent to develop a novel, general-purpose post-training method that outperforms a strong GRPO baseline on Qwen3-8B, with novelty defined relative to the field as of early 2026 and results strong enough for an academic paper. The work spans two task families — question answering (multiple-choice science questions from SciKnowEval plus a tool-use dataset) and competitive programming (LiveCodeBench with unit-test feedback) — with one method active across all of them; QA and tool-use tasks are graded on test accuracy at the one-hour and five-hour training-time marks using shared hyperparameters, while coding is graded on accuracy at and up to to a fixed budget of training generations. The agent may freely rewrite the algorithmic components of the provided verl stack (losses, advantage estimation, actor updates, reward functions, configs), but the infrastructure — rollout engine, sharding, data loaders, reward manager, model and kernel code — is fixed and restored before grading, so submissions must run against shipped versions of any file marked `[ARB SCOPE: FIXED]`. Strict rules govern data use: the provided pipeline decides which samples appear in a step, gradient is only taken on responses to the current step's questions, any auxiliary text must derive from current-step data, and ground-truth labels may reach the method only through the reward's scalar and feedback string, which never reveals the answer. Grading is robust against overfitting and tuning tricks: the grader re-runs the pipeline without the agent, performs a coarse sweep around declared hyperparameters, and tests on held-out datasets the agent never sees. Submissions require `train.py`, `run_config.json`, `method_card.md`, `results.json`, and trained model weights for each dataset at both the one-hour and five-hour checkpoints, with a strict rule that anything not provided scores zero; experiments are run via Modal GPU jobs with calibrated, comparable wall-clock timing.

item.title: 40. Clef-Omni: full multimodality, a faster Clef and a cheaper Clef-flash
item.description:
14 points by coloneltcb on 2026-10-09T19:05:31

Cloudflare has expanded its open-weight Clef decision-model family with Clef-omni, a multimodal model that accepts text, images, audio (wav/mp3), and video (mp4/webm) in a single API call—eliminating the need for cascading speech-to-text or media-splitting pipelines. Built on a Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B MoE backbone with the text-to-speech output components removed and trained via LoRA adapters with Brier-score calibration, it scores all modalities simultaneously in a prefill pass, returning text decisions in ~130 ms, images ~150 ms, and a 21-second video in ~1.5 seconds; benchmarks show it competitive with Clef, Clef-flash, and TypeSafe's Jev across BFCL, BANKING77, CLINC150, and workflow evals. Pricing is $0.15/M input tokens for Clef-omni, while Clef-flash drops from $0.09 to $0.038/M (now cheaper than Jev, though its hosted context window was cut from 64k to 24k, affecting only 0.24% of requests; self-hosted weights still support 256k). Clef itself was made 1.7–2.0× faster through serving-layer optimizations including a move to SGLang, with no new weights released. Cloudflare says internal teams already use Clef for spam issue detection on its GitHub docs repo, phishing moderation in EmDash, PII scanning for its DLP team, and malicious-domain detection for threat intelligence, and notes the entire Clef development took under a week.

item.title: 42. The Hetzner Cloud network stack – history and technical overview
item.description:
108 points by cnkk on 2026-10-09T12:20:55

A VM host in a Hetzner-style cloud must provide cloud servers with Internet reachability, private networking, firewalling, and configuration services. Private Networks connect servers, Load Balancers, and dedicated servers over a virtual network visible only to the customer, using VXLAN encapsulation with a unique Virtual Network Identifier per network, and the host network stack enforces that only attached members can exchange traffic. Cloud Firewall access control runs on the host itself, close to the server, because building stateful firewalls centrally would require extra hardware, network overlays to carry clean traffic, and complex highly available connection tracking. Server images use DHCP for dynamic IPv4 address and route configuration, so each host runs a local DHCP server for public and private interfaces, while cloud-init queries a metadata server at http://169.254.169.254/ for system and user configuration — such as IPv6 setup, triggering DHCP on private interfaces, and attaching cloud Volumes. This metadata server also serves other integrations including the CSI driver, hc-utils, Flatcar Linux's Afterburn and Ignition, and Talos Linux. Both DHCP and metadata servers run locally on every VM host for maximum resiliency and availability, alongside internal services that keep servers running, feed correct network configuration, and inform monitoring; the post focuses on the network stack itself.

item.title: 43. GPGPU-SIM – Cycle-Level Simulator for Nvidia GPUs with CUDA or OpenCL Workloads
item.description:
4 points by peter_d_sherman on 2026-10-09T22:27:23

GPGPU-Sim is a cycle-level simulator for modeling contemporary GPUs running CUDA or OpenCL computing workloads, and it bundles the AerialVision performance visualization tool and the AccelWattch configurable power model; both the simulator and power model have been validated against real GPU hardware measurements. The current release supports a subset of CUDA versions 4.2 through 12, and version 4.0 is compatible with the Accel-Sim framework, enabling trace-based simulation of NVIDIA SASS traces generated with NVBit. AccelWattch, introduced in version 4.2.0, replaced the older GPUWattch energy model and targets modern GPUs, having been validated against an NVIDIA Volta QV100. The page lists required citations for various features (Accel-Sim, CuDNN/PyTorch support and checkpointing, the Tensor Core and CUTLASS models, AccelWattch, CUDA dynamic parallelism, and AerialVision figures) and links to the online manual, AccelWattch documentation, a bug report form, and a Google Groups mailing list for best-effort support. Installation involves setting `CUDA_INSTALL_PATH`, sourcing `setup_environment`, and running `make`, with dependencies including gcc/g++, bison, flex, zlib, and the CUDA Toolkit; Ubuntu apt-get commands, a Docker image, and a VSCode/Codespaces devcontainer are also provided as setup options. Building can be done either with CMake (`cmake -B build`, then build and install) or with make, with a `debug` or `release` build type selected at environment setup (CMake instead uses `CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE`). Background is given on the project's origins in Tor Aamodt's group at the University of British Columbia, its evolution from a SimpleScalar-based design to direct CUDA/OpenCL execution, its use of Stanford's BookSim for the interconnect network, and the contributions of many researchers, including the Northwestern/Purdue/UBC teams behind AccelWattch, which builds on McPAT.

item.title: 44. Show HN: Apogee: Rebuilding Mozilla's Orbit, fully local and private
item.description:
64 points by zxdc7896 on 2026-10-09T07:36:19

Apogee is an open-source (MIT), local-first browser extension that summarizes articles, YouTube/Bilibili videos, PDFs, DOCX files, selected text, social threads, and pasted text entirely on-device — with no backend, API keys, accounts, or cloud uploads. It runs inference locally via WebGPU (Chrome/Edge and other Chromium browsers) or WebAssembly (default on Firefox), and can also connect directly to a local Ollama instance or self-hosted llama-server over 127.0.0.1 loopback. Features include timestamped video timelines, structured Markdown parsing of discussion sites (Reddit, Hacker News, Bluesky, Mastodon, Lemmy, Stack Overflow, etc.), Q&A with local passage retrieval, clickable grounded sentence highlighting, a persistent Chrome side panel, light/dark themes, custom standing instructions, per-page focus keywords, and translation into 32 languages. Privacy safeguards include zero data transmission to cloud APIs, loopback-only local model connections, optional anonymized SponsorBlock lookups (k-anonymity hash prefixes, disableable), and automatic exclusion of sensitive sites like Gmail, Slack, Discord, and WhatsApp Web from disk caching. Inspired by Mozilla's discontinued Orbit project, it aims to fix Orbit's design and privacy problems by keeping tokenization, inference, retrieval, and caching entirely on the user's device. The site also provides developer documentation: model reference tables, browser compatibility, Ollama and llama.cpp setup guides, privacy architecture, troubleshooting, and a Node.js fixture-based test harness for contributor-built site extractors.

item.title: 46. What should we tell our students?
item.description:
157 points by sajid on 2026-10-09T02:27:45

In this guest post on Terence Tao's blog, mathematician Álvaro Lozano-Robledo addresses undergraduate and graduate students who are losing confidence in pursuing academic mathematics careers due to rapid advances in large language models. Inspired by a distraught student's email asking whether AI will surpass human mathematical research ability within 5–10 years, he acknowledges that no one — not Fields medalists, mathematicians, AI experts, or frontier model companies — can predict the future with certainty, and warns that dystopian narratives are largely driven by AI companies with financial incentives ahead of upcoming IPOs (Anthropic in November 2026, OpenAI in early 2027), who publicize costly, heavily resourced successes while concealing the enormous expenses of failures. Despite these concerns, he remains highly optimistic, calling this the most exciting moment in mathematics since around 2000, noting that his own day-to-day work and that of colleagues has changed little, his research projects have tripled, and he has far more opportunities for student collaboration. He questions whether LLMs have demonstrated truly novel mathematical thinking, observing that none of their proofs so far contain "alien ideas" or arguments outside the existing literature, and endorses Nestor Guillen's "convex hull of ideas" hypothesis — the notion that LLMs operate within the combination of concepts already present in human mathematical knowledge, as illustrated by the Erdős unit-distance conjecture counterexample, which cleverly merged ideas from discrete geometry and algebraic number theory but arguably sat within reach of human mathematicians. He suggests that problems like the Riemann hypothesis, which may require ideas strictly outside this convex hull, remain out of LLMs' reach until humans introduce genuinely new concepts.

item.title: 47. Show HN: Babytalk: Offline speech to text and text to speech on ESP32
item.description:
11 points by tlack on 2026-10-09T21:33:56

BabyTalk is an MIT-licensed software library (by Thomas Lackner and Claude Opus 5.5) that gives ESP32-S3 and ESP32-P4 chips fully on-device, offline English speech-to-text and optional text-to-speech — no cloud, no internet, and no predefined command list. Unlike typical ESP32 voice projects that call cloud APIs or recognize only trained wake words, it transcribes any sentence using NVIDIA's Citrinet-256 recognizer (9.8M parameters, trained on 960 hours of audiobooks, outputting text directly via CTC), and wake phrases are any typed phrase, scored against the model's output with no training. It's usable from C (ESP-IDF components), MicroPython (stt/tts modules with async background transcription), or Erlang/Elixir on AtomVM (with its own audio drivers since AtomVM v0.7 lacks I2S). Memory footprint is modest: the default 4-bit model takes 6 MB of flash, read in place rather than copied to RAM, plus ~84.5 KB of internal RAM shared between STT and TTS, and a few hundred KB of PSRAM during use; an int8 model (9.8 MB, more accurate) and a better-sounding 2.4 MB "heart" voice for the P4 are also available. Four prebuilt models exist, including noise-fine-tuned variants that trade clean-speech accuracy (8.2% → 11.8% word error rate on LibriSpeech test-clean) for better noisy-room performance (58.1% → 42.7%). The core is MMRT, a custom inference runtime roughly 13× faster and half the size of Espressif's ESP-DL, using hand-written ESP32-S3 vector assembly, dual-core parallelism, per-layer weight loading, and layer fusion. Target uses include LoRa/Meshtastic nodes without keyboards (spoken sentences compress to a few dozen bytes, far less than voice codecs) and screenless speakers, with supported boards including the Waveshare ESP32-S3-CAM (reference), Waveshare ESP32-P4-WIFI6, LilyGO T-LoRa Pager, and Elecrow CrowPanel 7".

item.title: 2. Whistle: Speech to Text in 16.9 MB
item.description:
728 points by gmays on 2026-10-08T16:59:39

Whistle is a 16.9 MB speech recognition model designed for mobiles, wearables, robots, smart home devices, automotive and microcontrollers, running on the CPU with no dependencies inside the same C++ engine as the Needle text model. It performs three on-device tasks over 16 kHz mono audio of up to 30 seconds: transcription in seven languages (English, German, French, Spanish, Italian, Dutch, Polish, with automatic detection), word-level timestamps derived from the decoder's attention, and speech embeddings (one row per 80 ms frame). Its architecture uses a convolutional stem over 80-bin log-mel features, eight non-causal encoder blocks shared with Needle, and a decoder of eight Laddered Simple Attention blocks with 8:2 grouped-query attention and gated cross-attention to the encoder; a `--audio-depth` flag selects decoder depth from 2 layers upward while the encoder always runs all eight. Decoding uses five beams with length-normalised log probability, keyword biasing via an Aho-Corasick automaton, a 320-token cap and an 8,192-piece vocabulary plus seven language tokens; a loudness check short-circuits silent clips before beam search. Benchmarks show Whistle beating Whisper base and Moonshine tiny v2 on LibriSpeech, SPGISpeech, Earnings-22 and average FLEURS word error rate, while Whisper leads on TED-LIUM, AMI and MLS at 145.3 MB versus 16.9 MB; on an Apple M4 Pro CPU Whistle's time to first token scales with clip length (5.9 ms at 5 s, 36.3 ms at 30 s) whereas Whisper pads all input to 30 s. The engine ships prebuilt for seventeen targets and can combine speech and text models in one call, returning tool function calls and audio fields as a single JSON object; a Python package (`pip install cactus-needle`) provides transcribe, embed, playground and comparison tools. Weights are on Hugging Face, engine code in Cactus-Compute/needle3, source on GitHub.

item.title: 4. Yes, and
item.description:
376 points by Michelangelo11 on 2026-10-08T09:48:18

Carson Gross, a computer science professor at Montana State University, argues that programming remains a viable career despite AI, since it fundamentally amounts to problem-solving with computers and controlling complexity — but he warns that AI is especially dangerous for junior developers. He insists students write their own code rather than generating it, because you can't effectively read (and thus control) code you didn't write, and un-readable AI output risks creating "The Sorcerer's Apprentice Trap" of systems you don't understand. He rejects the analogy between AI code generation and the shift from assembly to high-level languages, since compilers are largely deterministic while LLMs often add accidental complexity through poor choices. Used correctly, AI acts like a great teaching assistant that unblocks learners stuck on environment/tooling issues — he shares an AGENTS.md file configuring agents for this role. Looking ahead, he expects raw coding prowess to decline in relative value while communication skills, business/domain understanding, software architecture, and effective LLM use become more important; seniors are well-positioned but risk "brain rot" from over-prompting, while juniors must resist "vibe coding" to build the intuitions needed for architecture. He describes his own LLM use — analyzing code, organizing thoughts, generating small or unpleasant bits of code, throwaway demos, and test suggestions — while never letting LLMs design his APIs. He views the current tough programmer job market as a temporary cyclical bust and advises students to ignore job boards in favor of the "four F's": family, friends, and friends-of-family, noting that nearly every large company has development needs even if the entry role isn't titled "programmer."

It’s about being able to reason about the relationship between source code and compiled program with formal precision. You can predict which changes in the source code will lead to which exact changes in the behavior of the compiled program. The same isn’t the case about changes to an LLM prompt and the LLM’s output.You could make an AI deterministic by fixing its source of randomness. That still wouldn’t allow you to reason about how its output will change when (for example) you add or remove a word in the prompt. The only way to find out is to run the LLM (= have the prompt run through the model and observe what comes out).That is the fundamental difference. Changes to source code have predictable and reason-able outcomes. You generally don’t have to compile the code and test it to know how precisely the change will affect the behavior of the compiled program according to the semantics of the programming language. A set theorist reacts to OpenAI's announcement that its models produced a Lean-verified argument that the Partition Principle does not imply the Axiom of Choice — a century-old problem on the author's own open-problems page, where they had promised a bottle of whisky to Sam Altman if it were solved. Despite that promise, the author declines to send it, arguing the preprint is muddled, oddly structured, uses unfamiliar terminology, contains oddly stated results (e.g., Lemmas 7.4 and 8.1), and cites unpublished lecture notes rather than published literature — quality that would warrant desk rejection from a journal. The author is not categorically opposed to AI in mathematics, viewing it as a tool whose proper role in the field is still being worked out (noting arXiv's rate limiting and the emerging norm of AI-use statements), but argues the burden of clear communication falls on the author, and OpenAI has not met it. Dropping hundreds of incomprehensible claimed "solutions" while the press release speaks only of "progress" amounts, in the author's view, to a denial-of-service attack on working mathematicians, who cannot be expected to stop their own research and teaching to decipher poorly written outputs. The author urges that if AI companies want to be genuinely helpful they should consult actual experts on the relevant topics. The post closes with the concern that hype leads the public, funders, and policymakers to believe mathematicians can be replaced by bots — confusing the tools with the craft — and that AI companies are demanding mathematicians adapt to their standards rather than the reverse.

item.title: 6. The value of not getting to the point (2015)
item.description:

Reflecting on a conversation with his college-age daughter—who wanted to "talk about something stupid" before getting to what was really bothering him—the author realizes that food, drink, and idle chit-chat aren't the point of socializing but rather rituals that build enough trust to overcome the inherent vulnerability of speaking. Because language is imprecise, feelings are hard to translate, and social penalties exist for saying the wrong thing, people need these conversational warmups before tackling sensitive topics. The author, a self-described introvert and get-to-the-point person who long assumed only he found conversation laborious, argues this insight explains Twitter's dysfunction: its 140-character format demands immediate directness, stripping away the trust-building rituals that real-life conversation has evolved over time, so the very problems those rituals prevent flood in. He notes that online conversational norms haven't had time to mature and that far more people are clumsy about online than offline communication. He concludes by announcing his plan to write explicitly about things that are widely intuited but rarely stated—acknowledging that this may insult the intelligence of readers who already grasp them, since the exercise is really an attempt to explain these matters to himself, and he accepts that as just another risk inherent in saying anything.

item.title: 8. Beauty in DVD Menus
item.description:
297 points by speckx on 2026-10-08T13:22:01

DVD interactive menus, a major selling point over VHS and LaserDisc, really flourished in the 2000s as the format matured and players became widespread. Technically, DVDs display video at 720×480 (NTSC) or 720×576 (PAL), derived from the D-1 and Rec. 601 standards, with metadata tags stretching this Storage Aspect Ratio to a Display Aspect Ratio for correct presentation — a legacy of the 4:3-to-16:9 transition that led designers to keep key menu items within a 4:3 "safe area." Interactivity was built from simple building blocks: 2-bit subpicture overlays with four colours drawn from a 16-colour palette, graphics-based subtitles, and a DVD Virtual Machine with just sixteen 16-bit General Parameter Registers for user settings and twenty-four read-only System Parameter Registers — a remarkably limited toolkit given the expressive menus produced. Typical menus offer play, scene selection, special features, and settings, ranging from static images to elaborate custom animations, hidden extras, and full DVD-based games. Notable examples include Disney's FastPlay (auto-playing content for accessibility) and EasyFind menus; Scooby-Doo 2: Monsters Unleashed's animated mining-town menu with two playable games; Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban's Knight Bus and Daily Prophet menus; Shrek 2's character-filled screen packed with games and extras; Rocky Horror Picture Show's iconic lips and curtain animations; Wayne's World's simulated cable-TV channel guide; and Doctor Who's Tardis-console menus full of hidden secrets. Looping clips and abrupt audio loops became a nostalgic fixture of the format. Today, however, both DVDs and more capable Blu-rays rarely feature inventive menus, replaced by generic templates as physical media declines in favour of streaming.

item.title: 9. Show HN: Making a flexible "neon" t-shirt with LED filaments
item.description:
158 points by scottbez1 on 2026-10-08T16:37:24

A maker built a wearable "LED neon" t-shirt in a few days for a neon-themed work event using flexible LED filaments (silicone-encased strips of tiny LEDs sold for retro-style lightbulbs). Because filaments can't be cut to length, the designs — a llama on the back from a single 1200mm 24V red filament, cursive text on the front, and straight warm-white border accents — were drawn as continuous paths in Inkscape and scaled to match available filament lengths; black heat-shrink tubing was used to block out unlit stretches between letters, and three 300mm 3V filaments were soldered in series to reach the front's ~900mm path. The filaments were sewn with loop stitches onto a cotton shirt backed with stiff cross-stitch fabric, using tissue paper as a tracing template that was later torn away. Wiring runs through magnet wire poked through the fabric to ribbon cables inside, powered from a USB battery bank and controlled by an ESP32: a TPS61169 constant-current driver with PWM for flicker effects on the front text, a cheap constant-voltage boost converter plus series resistors for the 24V llama, and a ULN2003A transistor array to under-drive the 12V borders from 5V, all packed into a 3D-printed enclosure with strain relief. It held up well at the event but, naturally, isn't washable.

item.title: 11. Bevy 0.20
item.description:
148 points by Philpax on 2026-10-08T22:57:50

Bevy 0.20 has been released on crates.io, contributed to by 227 people across 817 pull requests. Key highlights: Solari, Bevy's realtime pathtraced renderer, is now faster, more accurate, and runs on macOS via Metal, with ReSTIR made optional and off by default, plus new tuning knobs (world cache size, light sample count, temporal accumulation, bounce count) and support for Atmosphere and EnvironmentMapLight lighting; the dlss_wgpu crate now supports DLSS-RR 4.5, which requires updating the DLSS SDK. BSN, Bevy's new scene system, saw syntax improvements requiring @ prefixes for scene references, eliminating all template_value wrappers, allowing enums that implement Default and Clone without VariantDefaults (though every field must now be specified), supporting chained methods directly, and using -- to separate entities in lists; a new Ready event fires for each scene entity once its full hierarchy and components are spawned, enabling logic that depends on the complete scene. Bevy Feathers gained new widgets including Color Input, Scrollable List View, Dropdown Selection, Lazy Menu, a scrubbable Number Input with configurable limits, and headless Tab widgets with keyboard shortcut support in bevy_ui_widgets. Bevy officially adopted WESL (a standardized WGSL extension with modules, imports, and conditional compilation) for shaders, replacing its custom WGSL dialect. Also new: custom shader materials for Sprites, extendable 2D mesh materials, and a pan-orbit camera for CAD-like scene navigation. A migration guide from 0.19 is available.

item.title: 12. ADHD as a circadian rhythm disorder: evidence and implications for chronotherapy (2025)
item.description:
284 points by bookofjoe on 2026-10-08T20:42:16

Circadian rhythm dysfunction is a prevalent, clinically meaningful phenotype in a substantial subgroup of people with ADHD, and behavioral circadian interventions are proposed as low-risk adjuncts to care. Evidence shows insomnia affects up to 80% of adults and 82% of children with ADHD, delayed sleep-wake timing occurs in up to 78%, and dim-light melatonin onset (DLMO) is delayed roughly 45 minutes in children and 90 minutes in adults, alongside blunted and delayed cortisol rhythms, reduced pineal volume, and attenuated BMAL1/PER2 clock-gene rhythms whose weakening tracks with symptom severity. Intervention trials indicate circadian phase can be advanced: low-dose melatonin advanced DLMO by 88 minutes in adults (with a 14% symptom reduction) and 44 minutes in children with sleep-onset insomnia (plus 20 minutes more total sleep, though no short-term cognitive or behavioral gains), with long-term use sustaining benefits in 65% of a pediatric cohort; morning bright light therapy, alone or combined with melatonin, advanced DLMO by roughly 31 minutes to 2 hours and improved ADHD symptoms, with circadian phase advance emerging as the strongest predictor of improvement, particularly in winter given high seasonal depression rates (27%, highest in women). Behavioral sleep programs in children improved ADHD symptoms, sleep, quality of life, and functioning at six months, while exercise and multimodal chronotype interventions (fixed early wake time, morning light, evening light reduction, timed meals, caffeine and nap restrictions) shifted DLMO about 2 hours in "night owls" and warrant ADHD-specific trials. The authors propose a pragmatic behavioral-first pathway: routine sleep/circadian screening, phenotyping via chronotype assessment, sleep tracking and DLMO where feasible, fixed wake times, morning bright light, evening light restriction, regularized zeitgebers, and selective low-dose melatonin for confirmed or probable DLMO delay — calling for stratified trials to define responder phenotypes and optimize protocols.

item.title: 14. Scaling and benchmarking a critical message bus using a new indexing strategy
item.description:
41 points by eatonphil on 2026-10-08T17:39:26

Janestreet's internal messaging framework Aria (processing multiple terabytes daily) had scaling problems: tip recovery—where clients catching up to the live stream required filtering the whole message stream, often only a small subset of which they subscribed to—was driving some servers to 100% CPU, and initial recovery (e.g., after client reboots) could take over 13 minutes when it normally ran under 2.5 seconds, since Aria read up to 10x more data than needed. Intern Theodor Totev addressed both with indexing and tree-splitting optimizations. For tip recovery, instead of per-topic indexes (Aria has nearly a million topics), he built indexes per topic partition (topics sharing a two-segment prefix), with each index tracking message positions in the stream; clients' requests are served by an n-way merge using a min-heap. Profiling showed the heap was the bottleneck, so AI agents spun up five heap variants overnight—fast_heap_unboxed yielded a 2x speedup. Indexes are stored in a shared pool of 1024-entry blocks that are recycled as messages age out of the ring buffer, avoiding the ~2GB-per-partition memory cost of fixed-size ring buffers. For on-disk storage, Aria previously assigned topic subtree stores using a fixed three-segment heuristic, which wasted I/O when a low-traffic topic shared a store with a high-volume one; Totev replaced it with an adaptive algorithm combining greedy clustering with binary search, so high-volume topics get their own stores while small ones are grouped together. Validated via profiling tools, expect tests, property-based tests, Antithesis, and LLM-assisted code review, the indexing shipped to production with a 30% CPU reduction in staging workloads and eliminated multi-second tail latencies on non-indexed servers; adaptive splitting is in staging and heading to production.

Comment Link

Top Comments

  1. This is pretty funny to see, because every financial firm interview process I've seen involves some variant of solving a bunch of stuff with min heaps.Never before has a set of engineers been more primed to solve a problem
  2. Linear scans break at scale. Partitioning by prefix and using pooled 1024-entry blocks is the right move to prevent 2 GB worst-case index bloat.

Born in Toronto in 1950 and a former classics professor at Princeton, NYU and McGill, Carson is celebrated for work that moves fluidly between poetry, prose, translation and other art forms, drawing heavily on ancient Greek literature and mythology; her best-known book is *Autobiography of Red* (1998), a novel in verse reimagining the myth of Geryon. She receives 12m Swedish kronor (£900,000), becoming the 19th woman to win among 123 literature laureates, and will collect her medal and diploma in Stockholm in December. Carson, who has previously won the TS Eliot and Griffin prizes plus Guggenheim and MacArthur fellowships, revealed in 2024 that she has been diagnosed with Parkinson's disease.

item.title: 23. OLED burn-in test: 30-month update
item.description:
115 points by baal80spam on 2026-10-08T10:34:15

After 30 months (about 8,000 hours) of deliberately using an MSI MPG 321URX 32-inch 4K QD-OLED monitor exclusively for static productivity content — browsers, documents, spreadsheets, Photoshop and Premiere, 8–10 hours daily at around 200 nits, with no dark mode, no taskbar minimization, and only about half the recommended number of compensation cycles (865 completed) — burn-in has continued to develop but has not accelerated. The most noticeable artifact remains an inverse burn-in line down the center of the screen corresponding to the border between side-by-side application windows, which is now clearly visible on dark gray content and mildly annoying, though the left and right sides of the panel have degraded more evenly than in earlier updates. Taskbar burn-in is also more prominent, including visible degradation around the application icons and a shadowy blur in the bottom-right corner where Windows shows the time, date and status icons — though pixel shifting has prevented sharply defined lines, and this damage is rarely noticeable in normal use since it occurs where the taskbar always sits. Among subpixels, green has degraded the most and least evenly, blue is second, and red has held up best, which is why colors containing green show more burn-in; the display's color temperature has drifted down from about 6,440K to 6,292K, making it slightly warmer than new. Peak SDR brightness was unchanged at 243 nits for the first 18 months but has since fallen to 231 nits — a 5% drop occurring entirely within the last year — suggesting the compensation algorithm is gradually lowering overall panel brightness to offset uneven wear. The author concludes that OLED is still unsuitable for this kind of static productivity work, though the degradation has been gradual rather than catastrophic.

item.title: 26. Show HN: K10s – A Clickable Kubernetes TUI (Go, Bubble Tea)
item.description:
65 points by pierreneter on 2026-10-08T18:29:06

k10s is an open-source terminal UI for Kubernetes, positioned as a younger, deliberately narrower alternative to k9s with a mouse-and-keyboard philosophy: nothing is hidden behind memorized keys, since the actions applicable to the selected object are listed on screen and clickable, and a single ctrl+p search box covers both resource kinds and objects. It starts instantly by registering zero watches, with informers starting lazily per resource kind only when you view them. The tool covers 30 resource kinds grouped as Workloads, Network, Config, Storage, RBAC, Cluster, and auto-discovered Custom Resources, with day-2 commands on single keys (describe, YAML, logs with follow, shell exec, port-forward, metrics, edit, restart, scale, cordon/drain, delete), k9s-compatible scoped plugins via ~/.k10s/plugins.yaml, and a built-in AI prompt (ctrl+a) that injects the current context, namespace, kind, and selected object, supporting any OpenAI-compatible or Anthropic backend with no data leaving the machine unprompted. It reads the standard kubeconfig, ships an opt-in, clearly-labelled offline demo backend (`k10s demo`) with a sample cluster including a CrashLoopBackOff, offers self-updates via `/update` (checksum-verified, atomic, restarts into the new binary), eight built-in plus custom YAML themes, copy mode to release the mouse, and split commands: `/` for k10s itself (theme, settings, update) and `:` for cluster navigation in k9s vocabulary. Installation is via curl script on macOS/Linux (amd64/arm64), `go install`, or prebuilt static binaries including Windows; the page credits k9s and recommends it for users wanting the largest feature surface, while k10s suits teammates new to TUIs who need to find logs in ten seconds on their own.

item.title: 27. Sub-1-Bit LLM Compression via Latent Factorization
item.description:
83 points by brainless on 2026-10-08T13:29:46

This is the official code repository for LittleBit (NeurIPS 2025) and its successor LittleBit-2 (ICML 2026), methods that compress large language models into the sub-1-bit regime — from 1.0 down to 0.1 bits per weight. LittleBit works by factorizing each dense weight matrix into low-rank latent factors, binarizing those factors, and restoring magnitude information with lightweight learned scales, all while preserving the original model architecture at inference. LittleBit-2 improves on this by fixing latent geometry misalignment during initialization, using Internal Latent Rotation with Joint Iterative Quantization (Joint-ITQ) to align SVD-derived latent factors with the binary hypercube before quantization-aware training; it is enabled via the optional `--use_itq` flag and adds no inference-time overhead. The codebase supports quantization-aware training with SmoothSign and optional residual factorization for OPT, Llama and Llama 2/3, Phi-4, Qwen2.5 and QwQ, Gemma 2 and Gemma 3, and Qwen3, and includes commands for single-GPU and DeepSpeed multi-GPU training plus evaluation of local or Hugging Face Hub checkpoints (perplexity on WikiText2/C4 and zero-shot tasks like BoolQ, PIQA, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, ARC, and OpenBookQA). It recommends Python 3.12 and transformers 4.51.x for reproducing paper results, is licensed under CC BY-NC 4.0, and provides BibTeX citations for both papers.

Comment Link

Also no comparisons to FP4 solutions that are able to maintain or exceed perf on the same dataset 80% perf with a 4.25-4.5 big budget.I think more meaningful thing here would be a hybrid solution that went down to sub-bit representations when the informational representation does not need it (for example later layers) that still maintains task performance

I understand the obsession with low bit quantization, but it is empirically quite evident that it is not possible to compress models to less than 4 bit per weight without severe loss of capabilities².It may be nice as an experiment, but it is obviously a very inefficient route for model training: spending all the flops on a saturated model only to prune its capabilties.²As to why, I have seen few explanations. But the empirical evidence is there.

I understand that the interest in these extreme quants stems from wanting to maximize the capability the average user can get from a local LLM in this era of ludicrously expensive memory, but I wonder if this is maybe targeting the wrong axis?We've been seeing various optimizations towards streaming, that have been much more impactful in the local AI space, e.g. MoE models where the less busy experts are offloaded to slow RAM or even pruned entirely, engram tables that can be read from NVMe instead of sitting around in RAM etc.Maybe the trick with these extreme quants would be to increase the total parameter count while quanting individual weights, such that maybe the active parameter count comes down, or streaming weights from RAM or disk becomes more efficient, or cache behavior improves? Say, replacing a single 4bit/weight matmul with 3 1bit/weight operations that produce a much closer result than a single 1bit/weight matmul would.

item.title: 29. New CRAM method offers giant boost to compressed memory reads
item.description:
52 points by danny00 on 2026-10-08T13:11:41

CRAM is a new Linux memory-compression model developed by Gregory Price and his team at Meta, presented at the Linux Plumbers' Conference in Prague. Unlike existing options such as zswap and ZRAM, which function as swap-layer features, CRAM keeps compressed data entirely in memory, avoiding swap altogether. It works by using a private NUMA node rather than pretending to be a block device, which lets Linux retain its native memory semantics — including migration and ballooning — for managing CRAM. The result is dramatically faster reads: because compressed data is treated as RAM with full cacheline/byte access, reads run "at DRAM speed," delivering up to 452x the read performance of ZRAM (489 million operations per second versus 1.1 million in the worst tested case). Writes are slower since data cannot be modified in compressed form and must be paged and migrated back to the original NUMA domain, but even with a 20% write workload CRAM is still 5.4x faster than ZRAM. A "Chicken Bit" mechanism stops Linux from using CRAM during allocation management to prevent cascading failures (called a "poison storm") when writes outpace allocation. One unsolved problem remains: determining how much logical RAM is available given that compressibility varies wildly between data types, which is an active area of research. While aimed at large Linux servers, CRAM could benefit the broader ecosystem, including constrained devices like the Steam Deck, and may find its way into the kernel once implementation questions are resolved.
