item.title: 45. Forever junior: Skills AI can't develop for you
item.description:
73 points by brugidou on 2026-10-07T08:00:06

A junior software engineer at Criteo argues that AI agents are changing how engineers work but not eliminating the job, and identifies a real risk: if juniors let agents do all the work, Seniors may effectively disappear, leaving everyone perpetually junior. To reach Senior level, he studied what makes seniors effective — defending shipped code, arguing design choices, spotting when an agent is going off course, and knowing when to delegate — then focused on building human skills alongside his agent skills: curiosity (constantly questioning the agent's decisions, which mirrors Socratic "but why" learning), reviewing (learning his team's reviewing patterns from past code comments and feeding them into the agent's instructions), and "handwriting" (occasionally writing code himself instead of accepting the agent's output). He found that deliberately doing some changes by hand strengthened his architecture judgment, algorithmic understanding, token efficiency, and confidence, concluding that the agent should accelerate his growth, not replace the skills he needs to develop to become a Senior who can eventually write the comments that go into his own skill files.

item.title: 46. Strands Decider 2B: a small, open-source, decision model
item.description:
278 points by gmays on 2026-10-07T02:02:11

Strands Labs has released Strands Decider 2B, an open-source 2 billion-parameter "decision model" (also called a system-one model) designed for fast, local agentic AI workflows. Rather than generating arbitrary text like an LLM, decision models pick from given options and assign confidence scores, making them faster and more reliable at a given size — though incapable of reasoning through complex problems or generating text for chatbots, summarization, or coding. The architecture takes a Qwen3.5-2B pre-trained LLM torso, removes the language-modeling head, and replaces it with a small pointer head (roughly a million parameters) that scores answer options against an token, fine-tuned with a rank-16 LoRA adapter. The released version is v19, the result of many iterations, with all changes documented in the repo. On JevBench's public set, it ranks 3rd of 33 in the 2B class (1st of 30 excluding slightly-larger models) for accuracy and calibration (Brier score), with median local decision latency around 115ms on an RTX 3090 and about 153ms on an M3 MacBook. The 2B size was chosen to encourage experimentation on consumer hardware while remaining large enough for meaningful work — it answers all easy JevBench tasks correctly. Early use cases include model routing, tool selection, evaluations, guardrails, memory and context management, policy classification, and hybrid agents that use LLMs for hard decisions and deciders for routine ones. The model can be run via a `strands-decider` CLI (e.g., choosing which team handles a support issue, returning "billing" with 0.768 confidence), and the repo includes an example where a local Strands agent uses the decider as an intervention before tool calls — checking whether proposed arguments are grounded in the conversation and whether it's too early to call a tool — returning Proceed, Deny, Confirm, or Guide actions. Code, weights on Hugging Face, all training data, and scripts are available, and the team is building libraries for decision model integration.

item.title: 47. Show HN: NanoMuse – An open-source AI agent for your phone and computer
item.description:
57 points by ilreb on 2026-10-07T03:30:44

nanoMuse is a free, open-source (GPL-3.0-or-later) personal AI agent modeled on Meta's Muse concept, designed to run across every device you own — phone, desktop, and web console — under one account via a shared relay. Unlike cloud-VM-based systems such as Meta Muse or OpenMinis, nanoMuse runs locally on each device (Alpine Linux under proot on phones; DeepSeek Harness with Python on desktops), letting devices ask each other for tasks through the hub with approval flows, and letting you control apps without APIs via screen-based "Hands" control on Android and Windows. Key features include taking actions rather than just answering (Linux shell, browser, MCP servers, skills), stopping for confirmation before irreversible actions, running scheduled routines and goals when the app is closed, remembering user preferences in editable Markdown files, and answering in chat apps like 飞书, 钉钉, 企业微信, and Telegram. It supports the relay's free model allowance or 18 providers plus existing plans like ChatGPT and Claude; you can self-host the relay in about an hour on a VPS, use your own key with no server, or run your own runtime. The project is community-built, non-profit, has an associated arXiv paper (2610.08699), and the phone app is a GPL-3.0 modification of OpenMinis 1.13.

item.title: 50. Show HN: Terse, a Claude Code plugin that halves reply length by cutting filler
item.description:
16 points by lowenbjer on 2026-10-07T17:16:48

The terse plugin for Claude Code rewrites Claude's responses to eliminate verbose, stylistically cluttered prose. It replaces slogans, metaphors, "X, not Y" reframes, first-person narration, and other filler with direct, fact-first sentences, capping chat replies at 150 words and structuring answers as one sentence with the answer, followed by a list or table, at most one caveat, and no closing offers. The rules ship as an output style applied to the main agent, while a hook injects a condensed 576-character reminder into every prompt (costing about 145 input tokens per turn) to prevent style drift as context grows; subagents get the same rules via a hook since they run their own system prompts. Benchmarks against vanilla Claude Code show substantial improvements — on Opus 5.5, median reply length dropped 72%, output tokens fell 45%, style violations per 1,000 words dropped 90%, and metaphors and slogans fell to zero; Fable 5.1 saw 46% fewer words and 51% lower cost. The plugin also ships a context meter for the status line, colored by fill percentage (green below 37%, skull from 60%) to flag the retrieval degradation documented in Chroma's Context Rot report, NoLiMa, and Lost in the Middle, where attention quality drops well before a context window is full. It installs from the Claude plugin directory or GitHub via `/plugin marketplace add lowenbjer/claude-terse` and `/plugin install terse@terse`, and the rule set comprises 22 rules with 18 before/after examples. The README includes a side-by-side example answering a Flask timeout diagnostic question: the vanilla reply runs 636 words with six headers, repeated steps, and an offer to help, while the terse version delivers 180 words covering the scheduled-job hypothesis, pg_stat_activity sampling, pool arithmetic, and logging settings without any first-person statements.

item.title: 2. Decisions API is in public beta
item.description:
260 points by chiefstorm on 2026-10-06T20:57:25

OpenAI's Decisions API (public beta, GA expected in the coming weeks) evaluates text, images, or both and returns typed answers roughly 10x faster than the Responses API. It uses a dedicated POST /v1/decisions endpoint with three request parts: a model (currently only gpt-6-luna), shared input (a text string or user messages containing text and base64-inline images), and a list of named questions. Responses contain an answers array echoing each question's name, supporting three question types: **predicate** (checks a condition and returns a 0–1 probability the condition is true, useful for flagging images like visible product damage), **choice** (selects one value from supplied options with descriptions, e.g., routing complaints to billing, technical, support, or shipping), and **score** (rates input against ordered levels, returning a probability-weighted average of level indices, e.g., issue severity, which can fall between levels). The API is meant for classification, routing, and prioritization; use Structured Outputs with the Responses API for schema-constrained JSON generation or function calling for tool calls. Images must be inline base64 data URLs—hosted HTTP(S) URLs and file_id inputs aren't supported—and inputs can combine text and image parts. Each answer may be a refusal; SDK examples are provided for Python (3.26.0+), JavaScript (7.30.0+), Go (3.73.0+), Ruby (0.101.0+), and Java (4.78.0+), and the Playground lets you experiment before writing code.

item.title: 6. What Is Codemode
item.description:
69 points by Tomte on 2026-10-06T13:41:03

Pi 1.0 introduces MCP support via Codemode, an addition that reframes the author's earlier "code is all you need" argument that agents should use scripts rather than load custom tools or MCP servers into context. The piece explains that tools are token structures supplied by the harness and shaped by reinforcement learning, and that CLI/bash is favored because it composes easily and because models learn the file system from training — but bash can only compose programs that run, while some operations must be native tools injected by the harness, such as image reading (a multimodal model can't use `cat` for that) or spawning and orchestrating sub-agents. This leads to a "brains vs hands" distinction: the harness is a trusted "brain" running on one machine, while the "hands" execute tools in an execution environment that may be sandboxed separately (e.g., by Gondolin), with different file systems and trust levels. Codemode lets the LLM express and orchestrate complex operations on the harness side but not the execution side; it runs inside the harness sandbox (QuickJS in a WASM runtime, with no network, no file system, no timers, limited RAM, and the only escape being more tool calls), and its sole function is issuing tool calls from within a language — JavaScript — so the model can compose calls without spending context. Calling bash through Codemode instead of a plain tool call sends large outputs to Codemode structurally rather than into the transcript, and JavaScript unlocks concurrency and workflows, such as probing 5–10 items first and then writing a script to process the rest; Codemode can also stash state into the session transcript on the harness host for later invocations. Because Pi exposes internal model APIs through Codemode, the agent can reach things that don't fit traditional tools — image generation, and classifier models like Jev — illustrated by an

item.title: 8. AnyPS5: Port PS5 binaries to PC without emulation (87% system libraries mapped)
item.description:
231 points by Fe2O3 on 2026-10-06T23:28:08

AnyPS5 is a tool for automatically porting PS5 executables to Linux and Windows, using a relinker that converts executables into the target system's native format alongside implementations of system PRX libraries for dynamic linking — all without emulation or a separate runtime process. The project's shader recompiler produces valid SPIR-V (verifiable with Spirv-Tools), and unsupported or unexpected states throw std::runtime_error, printing the error to stderr before terminating. SDL-mapped game controllers are supported, with keyboard and mouse configurable via an anyps5-input.ini file. Dreaming Sarah, a 2D platformer, is listed as running at a stable 60 fps on a GTX 1050 Ti / i5-7500 system, and a game compatibility list tracks tested titles and known issues. The system library coverage percentage reflects functions declared in core/libs/prx only — a growing subset, not all PS5 functions. The project is licensed under GPLv2, is intended for interoperability, research, and preservation, and ships with no copyrighted software, firmware, cryptographic keys, or proprietary libraries; users must ensure any binaries they use comply with applicable laws and licenses.

Treg (treg.to, built by the Superdesign team) is an "OpenRouter for Tools" — a single base URL and token through which agents can call thousands of third-party API endpoints across SEO/backlinks, social and trends, people/company enrichment, ads, scraping, and image/video generation, billed per call from about a cent without requiring provider signups. The catalog spans tools normally locked behind expensive subscriptions (Semrush $139/mo, Moz, Crunchbase, Apollo) or invite-only APIs; treg holds the accounts and charges fractions of a cent per call. Two tool types are supported: the external catalog (served with treg's own key, a verified public route, or a team-supplied key — user keys are never metered and always take precedence) and team-registered tools such as stored API secrets, OAuth connections, vendor CLIs like Stripe/GitHub/Vercel, and SKILL.md-based skills, all registered via `treg scan`/`treg upload` and callable by every teammate's agent without the credential ever leaving the server. Usage is straightforward: install the CLI, sign in with GitHub or a token, then search the catalog by task (`treg catalog search "backlinks for a domain"`), inspect pricing and example responses, and call endpoints via `treg call` or by prefixing real upstream requests with the proxy URL; teams can run vendor CLIs locally or server-side (`treg run --server`), and skills are shared across agents including Claude Code and MiniMax. Additional features include a $1.00 credit for new teams, prepaid balances with HTTP 402 errors that agents can act on, an Enrich Arena and Web Arena for comparing vendor answers, prices, and speed on a live leaderboard, and a Claude Connectors MCP surface (treg.to/mcp/v2/) that separates read from write calls. The proxy relays requests faithfully, injects auth server-side, refuses unpublished-price endpoints, and supports self-hosting.

item.title: 11. OpenTPU – An open-source AI accelerator, developed by AI
item.description:
278 points by fsbonetto on 2026-10-06T16:23:25

openTPU is an open-source AI accelerator project built by AI, applying lessons from the auto-arch-tournament approach to hardware design and testing whether AI agents can help build the chip that runs their own inference. The entire accelerator lives in a single small monorepo: SystemVerilog hardware design, an instruction set, a bit-exact Python simulator, a kernel language and compiler, and host software for a real PCIe card (an Inspur YPCB-00338 with a Xilinx Kintex-7 xc7k480t and two DDR3-1066 channels, peak 17.1 GB/s). The design runs ten modern models with real weights — including LFM2.5-230M, Qwen3/Qwen3.5 variants, Gemma 4 E2B and E4B, LFM2-2.6B, SmolLM3-3B and Phi-4-mini — and produces tokens identical to the simulator, bit for bit. The machine is deliberately simple: a sequencer issues one instruction per cycle to a DMA unit, an int8 systolic matrix unit, an fp32 vector unit, a quantizer and a stream engine, with no cache and every data movement exposed as an instruction, so traces fully explain performance. The current production image closes at 133.33 MHz using LiteDRAM controllers (calibrated on-card in about 12 seconds without host help), a four-column systolic matrix unit, and a single bitstream for all models; decode is DRAM-bound at 82–85% of peak bandwidth, while prefill improved 1.3–2.0× over the earlier Xilinx-MIG image. LFM2.5-230M int8 reaches 59.0 tok/s device decode, 85.8 tok/s with 4-bit weights, and 4-bit quantization (FP4 with two-level block scales at 4.25 bits per weight, LM head kept in int8) cuts bytes per token by about a third and speeds decode 40–45%. Mixtures-of-experts models larger than the card's 4 GiB are supported by streaming experts from host storage, achieving 10.6 tok/s on LFM2.5-8B-A1B (98.5% expert-slot hit rate) and 3.95 tok/s on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B (62% hit rate, 153 MB per token over PCIe), both matching the simulator bit for bit. The host is nearly out of the path for decode, adding only 0.17–1.3 ms per token. Tooling includes otpu-chat, otpu-smi, otpu-lens (a browser-based profiler with roofline and cycle-level unit timelines), and selftest/diag commands; most work requires only Python and Verilator, the project is Apache 2.0 licensed, and open issues and pull requests are welcome.

item.title: 12. What's Earth's dominant species by mass?
item.description:
217 points by surprisetalk on 2026-10-06T12:40:03

Humans weigh about 350 million metric tons, roughly matching Antarctic krill (379 million tonnes), the most massive wild animal species, though cattle dominate all animals at 650 million tonnes (and pigs, at 140 million tonnes, fall below us). By carbon mass — the standard used in a 2018 study comparing kingdoms of life — animals total just 2 billion tonnes of carbon and trail protists, archaea, fungi, bacteria, and especially plants at 450 billion tonnes. Among domesticated plants, sugar cane leads with a 2 billion tonne annual harvest (about six times humanity's collective weight), beating the cereal grains; among wild plants, two boreal tree species dominate: black spruce, with over 11 billion tonnes in Canada alone, and Dahurian larch, with at least 8.4 billion tonnes in Russia. Since living black spruce wood is about 51% carbon, that single tree species holds nearly three times as much carbon as all animals combined — meaning humans may control the biosphere economically, but on biomass trees and other plant life vastly outweigh us.

California's State Bill 1406, signed into law on Sept. 30, 2026, closes the loophole that let wealthy residents register vehicles through fake out-of-state businesses—most commonly shell LLCs in Montana, which charges no vehicle sales tax and skips smog/inspection requirements. The old law applied a 50% test: a business owned mostly outside California could keep its vehicles registered elsewhere without paying California Use Tax. The new law expands the definition of taxable business entities to include partnerships, limited partnerships, and limited liability partnerships, and eliminates the 50% threshold entirely—now, if any shareholder, partner, member, or beneficial owner is a California resident, the entire business is treated as a California resident, making any assets kept in the state subject to state taxation. The bill also holds officers, managers, partners, and beneficial owners personally liable for unpaid taxes, interest, and penalties, with nonpayment potentially constituting a crime.

item.title: 15. When random is not actually random enough
item.description:
55 points by steveklabnik on 2026-10-06T20:12:05

Picking a random item from a set by taking a random 64-bit number and applying the modulo operator looks harmless, but it silently breaks uniformity: with 10 inputs and 3 choices, one option gets picked 40% of the time instead of ~33%, because the remainder classes don't divide evenly. The fix isn't just a better random_between(l, h) that samples an inclusive range uniformly — it's also a problem of choosing the right abstraction and mental domain. The author argues for a random_choice() API that takes options paired with explicit probabilities (like Python's weighted choice), since most random draws are really about picking objects with specific relative chances, not about generating a number. Because probabilities must sum exactly to 1.0, floating point makes this fragile, so the better default is relative integer weights — e.g. [(Blue, 10), (Red, 5)] — where each choice's weight is its share of the total, and where implementing the draw is intuitive: map the summed weights onto disjoint subranges of a uniform integer interval. The deeper lesson is that random variables have their own algebra, and non-linear operators like modulo don't preserve expected values or distributional properties, so you're working with the distribution, not the raw number. In practice, on the author's Antithesis fuzzing setup — where exercising code paths randomly drives test coverage — expressing discrete weighted choices directly proved far more useful, letting them bias case sizes (e.g. 88% small blobs vs. 12% larger streaming paths), steer search by adding options conditionally, and even model distributions like Poisson; after review they removed all uses of random_u64() from that code and banned new ones, and the post's takeaway is to ask whether the desired distribution can just be stated outright whenever you see a raw modulo-based pick.

A Uniform(0, 1) PRNG is the right primitive on which to base a PRNG library for arbitrary real-valued random variables because any real-valued random variable can be represented as an inverse quantile transform of a Uniform(0, 1) random variable. While I agree that only providing this primitive risks footguns as described in the article, I'm skeptical that providing a better UI alone would meaningfully reduce the risk of such footguns because availability and convenience is no guarantee of use if a prevailing attitude of users is that they know better and don't need it. Bisection search is simpler than rejection sampling or inverse transform sampling, yet it's common to see buggy, hand-rolled implementations of bisection search despite wide availability of library implementations with better UI ergonomics than PRNGs. item.title: 22. Mathematics of Geothermal Energy
item.description:
71 points by srameshc on 2026-10-06T13:05:26

Geothermal energy, drawn from the Earth's interior heat generated by planetary formation and ongoing radioactive decay, can be harnessed for domestic heating or to generate electricity via steam turbines. Heat rises with depth at a geothermal gradient averaging roughly 2.5–3°C per 100 meters, with molten rock at ~5,000°C about 6,000 km beneath the surface; heat escaping through fissures produces hot springs, geysers, and volcanic eruptions, and prime project sites lie along tectonic spreading zones such as the Pacific Ring of Fire. Geothermal heating has a long history — Iceland became a leader by the late 1920s, and modern heat pumps transfer heat between buildings and the ground — though large-scale water movement can cause geological consequences such as Venice's subsidence, prompting seismologists to model deformable porous rock to predict pumping-induced earthquakes. Mathematically minded researchers also use Lagrangian–Eulerian, stochastic, and geometric models to study geothermal processes, with applications ranging from neurosurgery to the isolation of radioactive waste, and they are working to expand the U.S. Geological Survey's MODFLOW groundwater model. Electricity generation began with a 1904 plant in Larderello, Italy, with Japan and the U.S. following in 1910 and 1921; geothermal plants drive turbines with steam at temperatures above 95°C (best output above 175°C), or use low-boiling-point fluids at lower temperatures. While capital costs are high, geothermal offers negligible fuel costs, low greenhouse gas emissions, reliable baseload output unlike intermittent wind, and no waste or finite-fuel issues unlike nuclear power; nonetheless, it still lags other sources due to a perceived scarcity of high-quality sites and technical, permitting, and transmission challenges, even as global production rose 20% between 2005 and 2010.

item.title: 24. The Early History of Smalltalk (1993)
item.description:
119 points by _reza on 2026-10-06T15:19:57

Alan Kay's 1993 historical account traces the origins of Smalltalk and object-oriented programming from the 1960s ARPA research culture of "human-computer symbiosis," interactive time-shared computers, graphics displays, and pointing devices, drawing on predecessors such as SketchPad, Simula, LISP, JOSS, Engelbart's NLS, LOGO, and the Dynabook vision of a personal, child-friendly learning computer. Kay frames Smalltalk as the first complete realization of a new computing paradigm—viewing the sixties work not as incremental improvement but as a qualitative shift—in which large problems become manageable and novices gain power, with user interfaces serving as learning environments along Montessori and Bruner lines. The essay covers the sequence of PARC projects (KiddiKomp, miniCOM, Smalltalk-71, overlapping windows, iconic and byte-code programming, Smalltalk-72, -74, -76, and the -80 release), the Notetaker, and the two bets on an Interim Dynabook and object orientation. At its core is the design idea that everything describable can be built from a single behavioral building block—state and process hidden inside an object, reachable only by message passing—giving Smalltalk a "crystallization of style" quality analogous to Leibniz's monads and a self-describing, recursive structure in which each object is a recursion on the whole computer, interconnected like thousands of machines on a fast network. Kay credits the project's success largely to Dan Ingalls and Adele Goldberg and the Xerox PARC Learning Research Group, notes that Smalltalk's contribution is primarily object-oriented design as a new paradigm rather than language features, and cautions that such histories are incomplete "feeble gestures" given the many contributors and rejected ideas that shaped it.

item.description:
434 points by simicd on 2026-10-06T11:59:01

Polars 2.0 ships with several major changes: SQL is now a first-class citizen, backed by optimizer and engine improvements (join reordering, common-subplan elimination, dynamic predicates/bloom filters) that put Polars ahead of DuckDB (1.5.6 and 2.0 alpha) and DataFusion 54 on TPC-H and TPC-DS 1 benchmarks run on 16-core and 192-core AWS machines, though Polars shows constant overhead at 192 threads on small data and limits itself to 32 threads for now. The streaming engine becomes the default for LazyFrame collect, which may change row-order for operations like joins, group_by, and unpivot unless maintain_order=True is set, and out-of-core spill-to-disk is enabled by default, starting to spill at ~80% of RAM with a 64GB disk budget (joins and group-bys are planned later). Polars also adds a native Map dtype mirroring Arrow's MapType (previously List(Struct)) with dictionary-like expressions such as map.get, contains_key, len, keys, and values. Stricter dtype checking and explicitness are emphasized, with collect_schema() enabling early validation and fast feedback useful for AI-driven development. Upcoming work includes better out-of-core support, scaling at high core counts, Polars Cloud as a distributed engine, and GeoPolars; a migration guide and benchmark repository are available, and issues can be filed on GitHub.

item.title: 27. The Query Transformation Pipeline
item.description:
14 points by gvsg-rs on 2026-10-06T22:09:14

Readyset is a database caching layer that replaces pull-based query execution with incrementally maintained dataflow: each query is compiled once into a graph of streaming operators (joins, filters, aggregations, projections), and upstream row changes propagate through the graph so reads become lookups into pre-computed materialized views rather than re-executions. Because the compiler imposes structural constraints SQL doesn't — binary joins with equality predicates only, no correlated execution, flat join structure, INNER/LEFT/CROSS joins only (no RIGHT or FULL OUTER), and strict GROUP BY/aggregation rules — syntactically valid SQL may not compile or may compile inefficiently. A multi-pass rewrite pipeline bridges this gap when a user issues CREATE CACHE: Block A normalizes the query (schema resolution, star expansion, column qualification, USING desugaring); Block B performs deep rewrites (ARRAY(SELECT) constructors become LATERAL LEFT JOINs with array_agg and COALESCE, ORM-generated self-joins are eliminated, top-level derived tables with ORDER BY ... LIMIT are inlined so LIMIT stays parameterized and a native Top-K operator can be deployed, and correlated subqueries — EXISTS, IN, LATERAL, scalar subqueries — are decorrelated into joins, with three-valued-logic probes installed when NULL semantics require preserving the TRUE/FALSE/NULL distinction); and Block C removes redundant clauses and parameterizes literals. Every pass is semantics-preserving, and inlining derived tables generally avoids materializing intermediate nodes that the engine would otherwise store exhaustively.

item.title: 32. OpenSSH 10.6
item.description:
105 points by torcete on 2026-10-06T20:41:39

OpenSSH 10.6, released 2026-10-06, is a complete SSH protocol 2.0 implementation including sftp client and server support. The release includes a notable statement that the team has received many security bug reports generated with AI assistance, many of which prove to have no real security impact under a realistic threat model, yet the team has repeatedly seen AI-reported bugs later discovered independently by human researchers—prompting more frequent releases so fixes reach users faster. Security fixes include stricter validation of sftp server-returned paths (Junghoon Cho), corrected GSSAPI credential handling and state reset in sshd (Moritz Theile), disabling of the LZ77 dictionary coder to mitigate plaintext-recovery side channels across multiplexed SSH channels, blocking of '$' and '\' in command-line usernames to prevent injection via ProxyCommand and Match exec, DST-correct certificate expiry times in ssh-keygen, limits on compressed payload inflation, full enforcement of the authorized_keys "restrict" keyword for tunnels, proper handling of "none" values in sshd_config Match blocks, and disabling of GatewayPorts and StreamLocalForwarding on platforms without file descriptor passing where sshd-session retains root. New features include the hybrid post-quantum ssh-mldsa44-ed25519 signature algorithm (requiring regeneration of previously generated experimental keys), a server-side WarnWeakCrypto option, FIDO user-verification preservation via credProtect, sftp's -p mkdir flag, a hexdump key export mode, fractional-second ChannelTimeouts, AgentSocketPath socket location configuration, pubkey "key ok" tests excluded from MaxAuthTries, and extended TCPKeepAlive support. Deprecations announced are scp -R (which will emit a warning, then be ignored) and future removal of support for platforms lacking file descriptor passing that require root for PTY allocation.

item.title: 35. Terraform Meets Proxmox: Lessons from a VMware Migration
item.description:
26 points by ultral on 2026-10-06T19:58:19

A case study on migrating a mature Terraform/Ansible/Packer infrastructure from VMware to Proxmox VE, documenting why a hypervisor swap is far more than a drop-in change. After comparing alternatives (XCP-ng + Xen Orchestra, Hyper-V, vanilla KVM), Proxmox was chosen for its web UI, native Terraform and Packer support, FC/multipath and live migration, and small operational footprint; on the storage side, the team tested local FS, NFS, shared LVM over FC, clustered filesystems, and Ceph RBD, ultimately combining NFS with FC and running fio benchmarks that showed VMware better for 4 KiB random writes while Proxmox was better for large sequential operations. The write-up then walks through the existing Packer → Terraform → Ansible pipeline and the Proxmox pitfalls encountered when rebuilding it, including non-bootable VMs from missing EFI/disk settings, SSH-unreachable guests due to VLAN tagging, hostname problems requiring cloud-init reboot logic, custom cloud-init being overwritten unless cicustom vendor snippets are used, race conditions between concurrent terraform apply runs (solved with remote state), the need for shared NFS storage to hold cloud-init snippets, HA configuration (target_nodes + hastate) so VMs survive host failures, and Terraform timing out mid-apply leaving VMs uncreated. The main lesson is that familiar IaC tooling does not automatically reproduce the old platform's behavior, so each template, VM initialization, storage, and failure-recovery detail must be deliberately re-engineered.

item.title: 36. How Fast is Python 3.15?
item.description:
63 points by Qem on 2026-10-06T21:52:57

An informal benchmark compares Python 3.15 (release candidate 3) against earlier versions back to 3.10, plus PyPy 3.12, Node.js 26.3, and Rust 1.97, using two test programs — a recursive Fibonacci calculation and a non-recursive bubble sort of 10,000 numbers — each run in both single-threaded and 4-thread mode. Results were averaged over three runs on a Linux laptop with an Intel Core i5 CPU; I/O-bound code and non-Python multithreaded runs were excluded. Key findings: standard CPython 3.15 is only marginally faster than 3.14 — about 3–4% on single-threaded tests and roughly 1–3% on multithreaded ones — meaning it is essentially the same speed as its predecessor. Historically, only Python 3.11 and 3.14 delivered substantial performance jumps, with other releases offering small gains or minor regressions. The standout result is the new JIT build in 3.15, which this year actually outperforms the standard interpreter: about 1.20x faster on single-threaded Fibonacci, 1.28x on single-threaded bubble sort, and roughly 1.2–1.5x on the multithreaded tests — an edge it did not hold in previous releases and that persists despite running with the GIL. The free-threading (GIL-free) build also shows strong gains on parallel workloads: about 4.5x faster than the standard interpreter on the multithreaded Fibonacci test and around 1.74x on multithreaded bubble sort, though it performs somewhat slower than the standard interpreter in single-threaded code. PyPy 3.12 remains dramatically faster than CPython across the board — roughly 5–18x — while Rust is by far the fastest overall (50–77x), and Node.js beats both CPython and PyPy on the bubble sort tests.

item.title: 37. Gleam doesn't compile to Erlang source anymore
item.description:
304 points by ingve on 2026-10-06T08:08:20

Gleam v1.19.0 has been released, headline feature being a complete rewrite of the Erlang code generator by Giacomo Cavalieri, which now outputs Erlang abstract forms — an intermediate representation in binary external term format — instead of Erlang source code, letting generated code be loaded directly and skipping the front half of the Erlang compiler. This significantly improves compilation speed (a benchmark of 100 modules with 100 functions each shows v1.19 compiling far faster than v1.17, outpacing Erlang, Java, Elixir, Elm, Rust, C#, and TypeScript, though only trailing Go), gives crash reports and stacktraces line numbers accurate to the original Gleam source, and raises overall compiler code quality; Gleam opted against generating BEAM bytecode directly because that format evolves with each VM release and would require reproducing decades of Erlang compiler optimizations beyond a small community project's resources, following Elixir's precedent of compiling to abstract forms. Other changes include flatter JavaScript output for case-expression decision trees (fewer branches for JS engines to optimize, thanks to John Downey), direct list construction for short list literals rather than array-to-list conversion (noted as particularly helpful for Lustre users), TypeScript declaration overloads that preserve type parameters for custom-type check functions, build-tool integration improvements to help Gleam packages compile under Elixir's Mix and Erlang's rebar3 (.app file generation, a --no-dev flag, and stdout/file output options for export commands, credited to Rodrigo Álvarez), and full language server support for field and argument labels — go-to-definition, find-references, and renaming — by Alistair Smith.

item.title: 39. System-level ad-blocking in Android
item.description:
66 points by birdculture on 2026-10-06T20:29:10

System-level ad-blocking on Android still works in 2026 despite the platform becoming more locked down, and because Android is owned by Google, which profits from advertising, customisation is increasingly resisted. All such methods work by overriding DNS: mapping known advertising hostnames to bogus IP addresses so requests for ads fail. There are four approaches — commercial ad-blocking DNS services (configurable via Android's private DNS setting), ad-blocking VPN services like NordVPN (often free as part of a privacy subscription), non-rooted apps such as AdAway that run a local VPN and DNS server to redirect name lookups (installable via F-Droid or by sideloading an APK, as Google increasingly discourages this), and rooted methods that edit the /system/etc/hosts file to map ad hostnames to 127.0.0.1 — made feasible on modern devices by Magisk's "systemless hosts" feature, which supplies a replacement hosts file at boot. Each approach has trade-offs: all depend on the accuracy and maintenance of blocklists, all require choosing trusted providers (a rogue DNS operator or VPN can intercept banking credentials), non-root apps create a bottleneck by routing all traffic through one app, and rooted methods require huge, up-to-date hosts files to avoid slowing lookups. No method is foolproof — some apps refuse to work or work poorly without advertising, some embed ads so no network operation exists to block, and Android's DNS caching complicates diagnostics, so customisable blocklists and community troubleshooting are necessary.

item.title: 42. Resurrecting iChat audio and video conferencing
item.description:
110 points by thepipetogrep on 2026-10-06T03:39:01

Chris Jones describes how he restored iChat AV's audio and video conferencing on Macs running OS X Leopard and Snow Leopard after Apple's servers died. In 2023, iChat calls failed because Apple's SNATMAP server — used to let clients discover their public IP and port for peer-to-peer RTP connections — had gone offline, causing clients to exchange private LAN IPs instead. In 2026, using LLM assistance to reverse-engineer iChat's networking framework from prior packet captures, the author and his friend Methodius recovered the SNATMAP protocol specification (a 16-byte request/response over UDP port 5678 carrying a nonce, external IP, and external port), wrote a Python server to host it, and tested the setup using two OpenWrt NAT routers running as VMs on Proxmox, with Jabber, web, and SNATMAP servers in a Debian VM to simulate the Internet. The easiest fix for users is to add the line `157.230.2.213 configuration.apple.com` to `/etc/hosts` on both the caller's and receiver's old Macs (port-preserving NAT required, so pfSense/OPNsense users must enable source port preservation), after which iChat calls work again; users can also self-host by serving `snatmap.txt` at the appropriate path pointing to their own SNATMAP server. The author is keeping a public server running for the few remaining users and notes that a modern Logitech C920 webcam works in place of the original iSight.

item.title: 44. Chrome's Response to Recent ccTLD Registry Hijacks
item.description:
23 points by agwa on 2026-10-06T17:59:32

Attackers hijacked the .gh, .sl, and .as country-code top-level domains, compromising the third-party ccTLDs rather than Google's own systems, and modified authoritative DNS records to obtain unauthorized HTTPS certificates covering Google and other organizations' domains. Google blocked these certificates for Chrome properties via CRLSets and worked with the issuing CAs to revoke them, then used Certificate Transparency log data to find and block additional affected certificates tied to other major brands and online services; Chrome users need take no action. Domain owners are advised to monitor CT logs across their entire domain portfolio (including parked and regional ccTLD properties), review recent CT entries if they operate a .gh, .sl, or .as domain, and publish restrictive CAA records with ACME account bindings to restrict which CAs and validation methods can issue certificates, since a CAA policy can prevent attackers from reusing cached domain-control-validation state to mint new certificates after a hijack ends. Google says browser-side defenses are insufficient and will pursue long-term HTTPS improvements, including reduced certificate validity and DCV reuse, through its Chrome Root Program and new Chrome Quantum-resistant Root Program.

item.title: 45. Stanford scientists found a way to regrow cartilage and stop arthritis
item.description:
45 points by kelnos on 2026-10-06T23:54:35

A Stanford Medicine-led study, published in Science, shows that blocking a protein called 15-PGDH — a "gerozyme" whose levels roughly double with age — can regenerate cartilage in aging knee joints. In mice, inhibiting 15-PGDH with a small molecule, whether injected systemically or directly into the knee, restored thickness to previously thin, deteriorating cartilage and produced the smooth hyaline (articular) cartilage needed for joint function. The treatment also protected mice from developing osteoarthritis after knee injuries modeled on ACL tears, which in people raise arthritis risk about 50% within 15 years; treated mice avoided arthritis, moved more normally, and bore more weight on the injured leg. Notably, the regeneration did not involve stem cells — instead, existing chondrocytes shifted their gene expression toward a younger state, reducing cells linked to cartilage degradation and fibrocartilage while expanding cells expressing hyaline cartilage and extracellular matrix genes. Cartilage samples from human patients undergoing knee replacement surgery responded similarly within a week, regenerating articular cartilage and declining in fibrocartilage and degradation markers. The authors caution that human efficacy remains unproven and clinical trials are needed, though a 15-PGDH inhibitor has already passed early safety testing for age-related muscle weakness. If successful in people, the approach could yield an oral or injected drug that regrows cartilage and reduces the need for joint replacement surgery — a meaningful prospect given that osteoarthritis affects roughly one in five U.S. adults and costs about $65 billion annually in direct care, with no existing drug that halts or reverses cartilage loss. The researchers hold patent applications on 15-PGDH inhibition for tissue rejuvenation, licensed to Epirium Bio, in which senior author Helen Blau is a cofounder and equity holder.

item.title: 46. Tapo (Rust/Python library) now speaks TP-Link's TPAP protocol
item.description:
129 points by faithraven on 2026-10-06T13:55:37

The unofficial `tapo` Rust/Python client for TP-Link Tapo devices has released v0.10.0, v0.11.0 and v0.11.1, adding support for the TPAP protocol (new in firmware 1.4.0, which caused 403 Forbidden errors) so that plugs, lights, power strips, hubs and some cameras work with the app's Third-Party Compatibility switch turned off — no code changes needed, since the client auto-detects the device's protocol. TPAP uses SPAKE2+ (RFC 9383), making recorded logins useless for offline password guessing and keeping past sessions private from later credential leaks; the library removes the obsolete legacy AES protocol but retains AES SSL for cameras and hubs. H200 and H500 camera hubs are now supported, pairing sensors and cameras, listing recordings by day, and downloading MPEG-TS clips, and plug Schedule and Timer features (rules firing at clock times or sunrise/sunset offsets, plus countdown timers) were added to PlugHandler. Also new: tapo-mcp v0.5.3 supports the camera hubs and devices with the compatibility switch off. Caveats include potential login lockouts after wrong passwords, unsupported devices like some C210s that still require the switch on, and breaking changes (legacy AES removal, renamed fields, Python enum comparison changes).

item.title: 48. Building Git infrastructure for agent-scale development
item.description:
7 points by edmorley on 2026-10-06T22:32:33

GitHub is rebuilding its Git infrastructure to handle the demands of agentic software development, as AI agents and large teams push repositories far beyond typical activity levels. Git activity on the platform more than doubled between September 2025 and August 2026, reaching 473.3 billion events per month, with 7.38 billion commits in September 2026 — over five times the previous year — and pushes growing 4.9x to 3.35 billion per month. Agent-driven workloads stress the system because each agent commits in tight loops, thousands of agents contend on a single ref for merges, every push fans out into thousands of CI and scanning reads, and repository maintenance costs compound as volume climbs. Today's architecture, Spokes, stores full repository copies on the local disks of multiple fileservers (five by default) and uses a quorum-based three-phase commit for reference updates; because those copies are both the durability mechanism and the read layer, adding replicas to scale reads slows every write, creating a ceiling at the highest activity levels. The new design follows three tenets: minimize coordination (only the reference update needs agreement, while object storage, validation, and scanning proceed in parallel, and compaction/GC moves off the serving path to background workers); decouple storage from compute (authoritative data moves to Azure Blob Storage, lightweight caching workers serve reads independently, failures recover like cache misses rather than requiring a full repository rebuild, and compute scales up and down with demand bursts); and preserve the workflows and controls developers rely on, including branch protection, required reviews, audit logs, and visibility. Internal benchmarks show up to 35x higher write throughput with read capacity that scales on its own. The migration happens while GitHub keeps running, with no maintenance windows or changes required of users, and a follow-up post will detail the architecture and its development journey.

item.title: 1. Beam: Reflection's 501B open-weight model
item.description:
425 points by Philpax on 2026-10-05T19:16:35

Reflection has introduced Beam, its first open-weight model: a sparse Mixture-of-Experts model with 501 billion total parameters and 23 billion active parameters per token, built for coding, reasoning, and agentic workloads. The team reports frontier-level inference efficiency, benchmarked via approximate FLOPS (2 × active parameters × mean generated tokens) and token counts on Terminal-Bench 2.1, Humanity's Last Exam, and DeepSWE, with data sourced from Artificial Analysis and DataCurve. A reinforcement learning campaign exceeding 100 million rollouts — including 80M used for training Beam's reasoning expert, far exceeding Inkling's 30M and MiMo's 753K — drove steady score gains on those benchmarks, with training remaining numerically stable even at one-day policy staleness, and the Pareto frontier improving first via token efficiency, then via expanded reasoning effort. To support frontier-scale RL, the company built a pool of nearly one million environments (mostly synthetic, covering software engineering, terminal use, coding, STEM, web search, tool use, and general knowledge), filtered for difficulty and quality and iteratively re-tested through RL — with data quality compromises found to cause capability plateaus. Infrastructure sustained 110K concurrent rollouts on average: fully asynchronous rollout generation with per-token version tagging, inference-to-training GPU ratios of 3.9:1 to 5.4:1, median ~12-second weight distribution (75% less cross-rack traffic, 2.2× faster fleet adoption via RoCE/NVLink hierarchy), 71 inference incidents absorbed without stopping training (0.02% of serving GPU-minutes lost), up to 170K concurrent sandboxes with 90% ready in under 10 seconds, dynamic packing keeping batches 99.99% full, and per-token observability plus reward-integrity re-screening. Beam was pretrained on 23.8 trillion tokens using in-house quality classifiers, fine-grained tiering, per-language code filters, and a high-throughput vision-language OCR pipeline for PDF/STEM content, with code and technical data repeated across the training horizon; conventional curation would have missed ~1.8 trillion high-quality tokens including 87% of curated web-code tokens. Pretraining ran end-to-end in under four weeks on 6,144 NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 GPUs using a largely in-house infrastructure stack, achieving 92.3% goodput late in the run with nine semi-automatic rewinds; the pretraining recipe scales predictably across four orders of magnitude in compute, is Pareto-optimal in loss-vs-compute on decontaminated code and web validation data among comparable open base models, maintains near-uniform expert utilization (busiest expert at 1.04×), and keeps residual stream RMS bounded across all 52 layers.

This page describes an offline, browser-based route planner for San Francisco that computes walking and cycling routes over 160,000 street segments using USGS 1 m lidar elevation data and the Overture/OpenStreetMap street graph. A slider spans the entire trade-off between route distance and climbing, displaying every route that isn't beaten on both metrics — from the shortest path to the flattest worthwhile option (where a foot of climb counts as 200 ft of extra walking, past which routes stop being practical); sliding right never shortens a route or adds climbing. Climbing is measured as cumulative elevation gain rather than endpoint net difference, stairways are allowed on foot but excluded on bikes, faint lines indicate alternative routes along the way, and place search works offline using built-in data for San Francisco's intersections, places and addresses, with source code, data and full analysis linked from the page.

item.title: 3. Opus 5.5 agents discover two room-temperature magnetic semiconductor candidates
item.description:
332 points by outlier99 on 2026-10-05T21:00:21

Luttinger compensated magnets are antiferromagnets whose up and down atomic moments cancel to zero, yet — because the two sublattices sit in inequivalent environments — their electrons are still sorted by spin at the band edges, combining the zero stray field and fast switching of antiferromagnets with the spin-readability of ferromagnets; the goal for memory is a semiconductor with a wide "spin window" (the energy range at a band edge where every state has the same spin) far exceeding room-temperature thermal fluctuations (~26 meV). Using density functional theory simulations (PBE+U and the more accurate HSE06), an author and a team of AI agents identified two candidates: a newly designed oxide, YBaMnFeO₅, predicted to be a semiconductor with a 2.35 eV gap and spin windows of 1.0 eV (holes) and 1.4 eV (electrons), magnetically ordered up to roughly 420–490 K, but whose necessary Mn/Fe checkerboard ordering disorders around 950 K — making it hard to synthesize in the required form; and KV[Cr(CN)₆], first prepared in 1999, which belongs to the Prussian blue family, has a predicted 2.1 eV gap with 2.6 eV and 1.6 eV spin windows, and whose 1999 sample stayed magnetically ordered up to 376 K (103 °C), with its crystal structure locking chromium to the carbon ends and vanadium to the nitrogen ends of the cyanide ligands — the very site inequivalence the oxide lacks — making it a likely room-temperature Luttinger compensated semiconductor that had effectively been hiding in plain sight (a 2008 study had even plotted its spin-sorted band edges without remarking on the significance). Caveats are flagged: the only existing sample is a water-containing powder with a small residual moment (0.125 Bohr magnetons per formula unit rather than zero), the two computational methods disagree on how much the water degrades the effect, and neither the band gap nor the spin sorting has yet been measured; the next step is to remake KV[Cr(CN)₆] and test the spin sorting directly. All input files, raw outputs and analysis code are shared in a public GitHub repository (github.com/spicylemonade/compensated-magnet-ledger) for independent verification.

Comment Link

  1. > We’re all used to two types of magnet. The common one, the fridge magnet, is ferromagnetic — its atomic magnets all point the same way (up or down), adding their magnetic effects. The less well known one, the antiferromagnet (AF), has neighbouring atomic magnets that point opposite ways and exactly cancel out magnetically.This is a very bizarre introduction. People encounter diamagnets (e.g., copper) and paramagnets (e.g., aluminum) way more than they encounter antiferromagnets. I don't know why you'd ever cast magnetism as a false binary between ferromagnets and antiferromagnets, without acknowledging any other types of magnetic order.(I did a PhD in magnetic materials)Edit: I'll add that whether an antiferromagnet is useful, say, for exchange biasing a ferromagnetic thin film, depends on many factors. Just looking at antiferromagnetism alone you've got collinear vs non-collinear, G-type vs A-type vs C-type, commensurate vs incommensurate, and isotropic vs anisotropic; and all of that interacts with the interface structure, yada yada yada. It would be helpful if the authors elaborated on the expected properties of these materials. I personally don't know what people want room-temperature magnetic semiconductors for, but I'd be curious to learn what set of properties they think would be useful.

item.title: 4. Example.com just launched the biggest redesign in decades
item.description:
207 points by jgx0 on 2026-10-05T22:55:11

example.com is a domain reserved by IANA for use in documentation examples and not for general-purpose endpoints like availability testing. A redesign on 28 September 2026 added multi-language support, cycling through English, Arabic, Chinese, French, Russian and Spanish every 5 seconds via JavaScript, each character wrapped in a span with an incrementally delayed 0.4s opacity transition, plus an SVG book icon. IANA says the changes are aimed at reducing bandwidth for a heavily trafficked placeholder page and improving its utility, with most automated traffic not fetching the JavaScript file. The site launched in January 1999; the earliest viewable 2002 version was a table-based page listing reserved domains served by Apache 1.3.22, with recognizable messaging arriving in March 2002 and an RFC 2606 citation added in February 2003. Other milestones include example.edu joining the list in 2010, a 2011 redirect to IANA's site that ended in 2013 with a major redesign on the EdgeCast CDN, a 2019 font and copy update, a 2025 infrastructure change, a 2025 redesign with minified HTML, a December 2025 migration to Cloudflare, and minor 2026 HTML and favicon tweaks. The page has repeatedly warned against relying on example.com for testing and monitoring, and the authors' own uptime data shows the server occasionally failing to respond, suggesting users test infrastructure they control instead. Changes occur sporadically, from back-to-back months to gaps of up to seven years.

item.title: 5. Dust: Pretraining Transformers Without Backpropagation
item.description:
165 points by E-Reverance on 2026-10-05T21:15:07

Dust is a zeroth-order optimization method from Q Labs Research for pretraining transformer language models without backpropagation. It adds Gaussian noise to the output of each linear layer, independently at every token, so each token acts as a member of a "virtual population" and a single forward pass evaluates thousands of members in parallel — avoiding the cost of materializing separate weight-perturbed models as in weight-space evolution strategies like EGGROLL. Each token's noise is rewarded by its change in loss; reward-weighted noise averaged over draws estimates the layer output error, whose outer product with the layer input gives the weight gradient, with attention layers credited through estimated error at the attention output. A generic credit assignment rule applies different token-level rewards to different layer types within a transformer block. Except for the 2L residual mixing scalars (trained via ordinary weight-space ES), all weights are trained this way. The authors report Dust is competitive with backprop at pretraining, exceeding it in multiple settings at large populations, and is roughly 10³–10⁴× more compute-efficient than a transformer implementation of EGGROLL from 1M tokens upward. Contrary to conventional wisdom, larger models are more population-efficient: a 243M-parameter model beats a 120× smaller one at most population sizes, suggesting overparameterization provides a larger, better-conditioned search space. Gradient estimates align better with backprop's as population grows and remain aligned at all scales tested up to 1B tokens. The authors frame this within the "bitter lesson" argument that generic compute-heavy search methods may eventually beat architectures co-evolved around differentiability, while noting they do not yet aim to replace backprop on compute efficiency and leave architectures such as externally guided or looped transformers to future work.

Comment Link

Top Comments

  1. Every few years, a derivative-free neural network optimization algorithm gets some hype. I'd bet my life savings that none of them ever make an impact.Derivative-free optimization can be useful for genuinely discontinuous objectives [1], but common neural network objectives are smooth and/or Lipschitz.The gradient is useful. Instead of trying random directions and hoping that one of them is an improvement, it tells you where to go. The more parameters you have, the more useful it becomes.A strict complexity gap between gradient-based and derivative-free Lipschitz convex optimization has been suspected for decades and recently proved (using AI, [2]). Neural net optimization is nonconvex, but not radically different.IMO, a more promising direction is gradient-based optimizers specialized to the neural network structure, like Muon [3].[1] https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.00817[2] https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.13335[3] https://jeremybernste.in/writing/deriving-muon
  2. I'm skeptical as to whether zeroth-order methods really lend themselves to a Bitter Lesson argument. First-order methods don't explore the loss landscape optimally, but the loss function tends to be nonconvex, and zeroth-order methods don't address that issue head on. Dust smooths, and so do applicable first-order methods. Remove the nonconvexity issue, and I suspect Dust's purported advantages evaporate (based on published theoretical work), so it's pretty odd to me that the paper never discusses convexity.I could buy that this method scales better than previous zeroth-order methods, and that's interesting, but it doesn't seem like enough of a moat to keep improved first-order methods from drinking its milkshake, except in cases where a zeroth-order method is already a primary option: the network needs to call a simulator that doesn't expose gradient-like information. (In cases where gradients don't exist, I'd still argue for other options, e.g., Clarke-generalized gradients where applicable, so long as those can be computed with the available information. I know this technology has been published for automatic differentiation, so I would imagine it could be incorporated into backprop and used with a suitable optimization algorithm.)

For package management they use FNM instead of NVM and PNPM instead of NPM, aliasing `npm`/`npx` to `pnpm`/`pnpx`, configuring `minimumReleaseAge: 1440` and `trustPolicy: no-downgrade` in `pnpm-workspace.yaml` to delay potentially malicious packages, and self-hosting a Forgejo instance with PNPM trust settings to work around lost package "provenance." Node can run TypeScript directly but deliberately refuses to strip types in `node_modules`, so the author bundles TS with Tsdown. The author also declares Deno effectively dead: its innovation stalled, half the staff were laid off, it leaned into AI products, and recurring issues (broken ZSH integration, JSR rate-limiting, concurrent HTTP request bugs) finally pushed them to `brew uninstall deno`.

Carli Michelle Heller, a Bonita Springs, Florida woman, faces a second-degree felony charge for making a written threat of violence after using Anthropic's Claude as a diary and allegedly writing on September 26 that she planned to "shoot up" the Sheriff's office. Claude's safety systems flagged the entry and escalated it to a human reviewer, who deemed it a credible threat and reported it to law enforcement under Anthropic's policy of disclosing user information in limited emergencies involving potential death or serious injury. Deputies detained Heller without incident, and she was charged under Florida Statute 836.10, which criminalizes sending or transmitting written or electronic threats to kill, injure, carry out a mass shooting, or commit terrorism, provided another person may view the communication. The incident highlights broader concerns about AI chatbot privacy and AI companies' liability: last month, British Columbia sued OpenAI and Sam Altman alleging the company failed to prevent a mass shooting after safety staff flagged a suspect's conversations about gun violence but did not alert police because they fell below the legal referral threshold, while Florida also sued OpenAI alleging ChatGPT contributed to real-world harms including the 2025 Florida State University shooting. Additional reports revealed that human contractors reviewing Microsoft Copilot's image editor can access users' prompts, uploaded photos, and AI-generated edits, some containing sexual, disturbing, or potentially illegal material.

item.title: 8. Web Search API
item.description:
534 points by tosh on 2026-10-05T10:47:06

Cloudflare's Web Search API is now in beta, letting AI agents and applications search the live Internet and ground responses in up-to-date information instead of relying on a model's training cutoff or guessed URLs. At launch, users can choose among three providers — Ceramic.ai, Exa, and Linkup — all of which support Zero Data Retention for requests made through Cloudflare and have committed to Cloudflare's verified bot crawling standards. The API runs through AI Gateway, so search requests appear in gateway logs and are billed to AI Gateway credits at each provider's list API price with no markup, though users can also supply their own provider API key. Calls can be made via a REST endpoint at `api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/accounts/{account_id}/ai/websearch/` (POST, with query, provider, and limit parameters) or from a Worker using the `env.AI.websearch` binding, passing a gateway ID, query, provider, and limit to retrieve JSON results. Getting started is documented in the "How to use Web Search API" guide.

item.title: 10. ChatGPT is adding real cartoonists' signatures to fake New Yorker cartoons
item.description:
403 points by rdmuser on 2026-10-05T22:46:45

After the deaths of Dolly Parton and Tim Curry in late August, a "New Yorker-style" cartoon of the two at the pearly gates went viral on social media — but it wasn't drawn by cartoonist Brendan Loper, despite bearing his "BLOPER" signature; it was generated by ChatGPT, which had been prompted simply for a New Yorker-style cartoon. Loper's pen name wasn't an isolated case: the article documents more than 15 New Yorker cartoonists, including Harry Bliss, Emily Flake, Joe Dator, and even long-deceased contributors like Saul Steinberg and Warren Miller, whose signatures ChatGPT reproduced without permission or payment, with some AI outputs also reproducing the magazine's logo. The cartoonists say the forged signatures feel like impersonation and a violation of personhood more than mere style mimicry — the signature is their certificate of authenticity and brand — and they argue the tools are designed to undercut creative labor. OpenAI said it appreciates flags of "unintended behavior" and began returning a guardrail warning when notified, though some signed outputs continued. There is no public licensing basis for the training: Condé Nast's 2024 OpenAI deal excluded LLM training on cartoons, and New Yorker cartoonists retain copyright under spec-based contracts that don't permit AI licensing; how the signatures were ingested is unknown, though unsealed documents in the New York Times v. OpenAI lawsuit show OpenAI knowingly scraped around publishers' paywalls. Legal experts say copyright claims are hard because ChatGPT mimics general style rather than copying specific works, while a "right of publicity" claim might exist but would require proof of commercial use — and cartoonists point to The Baltimore Sun, which fired a veteran editorial cartoonist and now regularly publishes OpenAI-generated cartoons, as evidence the threat is already displacing paid work.

item.title: 11. Samon: Designing a Zen Garden Raking Puzzle
item.description:
41 points by networked on 2026-10-05T23:35:35

This page is the appendix to "Samon" (砂紋, "sand crest"), a design document and playable prototype for a Zen sand garden puzzle game, in which the player rakes a garden in a single stroke to recreate patterns the way Zen monks do — with rules such as ripple stones, wave bands, ichimatsu blocks, grooves, pebbles, side gates, fixed rake starts, and no-U-turn constraints, and a "par" number of turns for each garden. It packages everything behind the document: a 225-file, 1.8 MB .zip download (SHA-256 6b7cf492b56edb0935ce3b937b2e242ad3a79179630878faa9ccd57d03b35f24) covering the exact DFS solver (zgsolve.c), the garden model and brute-force checker (zg.py), an independent CP-SAT model for par proofs (zcp.py), a deductive difficulty grader, level and campaign generators, figure and table renderers, a verify_doc.py script that re-derives every number in the document, cross-validation tests, poem files, sound assets, and a single-page, dependency-free prototype built from a template with build scripts. The game contains 7 worlds and 148 gardens (72 on the main path with teaching, trap, calm, and capstone roles, plus 76 extras), a year of 366 daily gardens, poems paired to gardens, and shareable raking codes and progress encoded in URL hashes keyed by a 32-bit hash of each garden's layout so links survive reordering. Build instructions and Playwright tests for the prototype are provided, along with a note that the page itself and the prototype's two generated pages are not in the zip.

item.title: 12. Ephemeral Testing
item.description:
52 points by ibobev on 2026-10-05T23:06:36

Ephemeral testing is a proposed AI-era quality-assurance method for evaluating a software component without testing it directly. Instead, you have an AI agent build a throwaway application or layer on top of your component — or of code the agent itself produced — and then have that agent test what it built. The layered software is discarded afterward, acting as a disposable integration test. Because the temporary layer exercises the foundation's API, invariants, and error handling, the failures it produces serve as evidence about the underlying code rather than the agent: a library with a clean API, stable invariants, and good documentation lets the agent build something that works quickly, while hidden state, surprising defaults, or incomplete docs lead to patches and failures. The process can be repeated with different agents and different tasks against the same foundation, so instead of building the core while speculating about future needs, you simulate those needs by actually building them on the fly. The author applies this approach to his own projects, using AI to prototype upcoming features, and reports it working well so far, arguing that some stable foundation is still necessary even when AI can rebuild everything on demand.

Comment Link

Top Comments

  1. This is an interesting idea. It's effectively what a good software engineer already does in their head, except it's doing it with a real compiler.Richard Gabriel wrote something that has really stuck with me:> Abstractions must be carefully and expertly designed, especially when reuse or compression is intended. However, because abstractions are designed in a particular context and for a particular purpose, it is hard to design them while anticipating all purposes and forgetting all purposes, which is the hallmark of the well-designed abstractions.This is one of my favourite quotes on abstraction, because “anticipating all purposes and forgetting all purposes” is such a good summary of what goes into abstraction design.A language model in an agentic harness cannot (yet) do this at the same level as a good software engineer, but the advantage they have is speed of token generation, so they can actually build the things the engineer tries to imagine, and verifying those is easier. Flock's automated license plate reader cameras are widely deployed by law enforcement yet remain largely opaque to the public, which struggles to learn where cameras are installed, who accesses the footage, how often, and for how long data is retained. Flock offers optional "transparency portals" that agencies can use to publish statistics on camera counts, vehicle scans, and police searches, but uptake is minimal: in Texas, where hundreds of agencies use Flock, only 59 have portals and just 16 share data publicly. Advocates and lawyers, including Institute of Justice attorney Michael Soyfer, who is litigating Fourth Amendment cases over Flock abuses, warn that without court-imposed warrant requirements or stronger state and local transparency mandates, the network will keep tracking people in ways the public cannot fully understand. Soyfer also cautions that AI could amplify the problem by automating policing practices the public already resents—for example, enabling officers to set alerts for "suspicious" travel patterns, such as federal agents monitoring cars making repeated cross-border day trips to create pretexts for stops, interrogations, and searches.

item.title: 16. Making a GTK application in Haskell, part 1
item.description:
154 points by Vosporos on 2026-10-05T14:23:47

This first installment of a multi-part tutorial shows how to build a todo-list desktop application in Haskell using GTK 4 and libadwaita, aimed at intermediate Haskellers. It introduces Adwaita as GNOME's design-language library (encoding accessibility and the Human Interface Guidelines, with responsive light/dark theming) and the haskell-gi toolkit, which auto-generates Haskell bindings from GTK libraries. The article walks through creating an `Adw.Application` and an `ApplicationWindow` with a `HeaderBar` and `ToolbarView`, then applies the Elm Architecture to the app: a `Model` holding a `Map TodoId Todo` plus a `nextId`, a `Message` sum type (`Add Text`, `SetDoneStatus`), and a pure `update` function returning a new model and a list of `Effect`s — notably a `Save` effect that fires only when the todo set actually changes, as demonstrated interactively in GHCi. The view layer is composed from Adwaita and GTK widgets (Box, ListBox, EntryRow, ActionRow, Clamp, ScrolledWindow, ToolbarView), with an entry row dispatching `Add` messages and a footer label showing the task count. Finally, the runtime ties the three parts together: an `IORef` stores the current model, and `dispatch`/`step` use `GLib.idleAdd` to schedule the update, re-render the view, and set it as the window's content. The full project is available on GitHub, with part 2 promised to add more todo-list features.

item.title: 18. Linux containers in 500 lines of code (2016)
item.description:
121 points by mkornaukhov on 2026-10-05T14:09:15

This code listing shows how to drop Linux capabilities when sandboxing a container, using both `prctl(PR_CAPBSET_DROP, ...)` to remove them from the bounding set and libcap's `cap_set_flag(..., CAP_INHERITABLE, ..., CAP_CLEAR)` to clear them from the inheritable set. Each dropped capability is justified with its security risk: CAP_AUDIT_CONTROL/READ/WRITE expose the kernel audit system (CAP_AUDIT_READ is not namespaced, and CAP_AUDIT_WRITE could falsify logs or DoS the audit system); CAP_BLOCK_SUSPEND and CAP_WAKE_ALARM can interfere with system suspend; CAP_DAC_READ_SEARCH enables reading arbitrary files via `open_by_handle_at` (used to break out of Docker in 2014); CAP_FSETID lets setuid binaries keep their setuid bit when modified, leaving dangerous setuid-root binaries on disk; CAP_IPC_LOCK can be used for DoS; CAP_MAC_ADMIN and CAP_MAC_OVERRIDE bypass system-wide mandatory access control (AppArmor, SELinux, SMACK); CAP_MKNOD lets a process recreate real device files, e.g., remounting the host hard disk; CAP_SETFCAP could let an altered executable gain capabilities and be run by any unsandboxed user; CAP_SYSLOG enables destructive syslog actions and leaks kernel addresses, defeating KASLR; CAP_SYS_ADMIN grants many behaviors (mount, etc.) that are deliberately skipped as too complex; CAP_SYS_BOOT permits reboot and kexec loading; CAP_SYS_MODULE allows loading kernel modules; CAP_SYS_NICE can raise priority and DoS the host scheduler; CAP_SYS_RAWIO grants access to host memory and I/O ports; CAP_SYS_RESOURCE can bypass kernel-wide limits; CAP_SYS_TIME can alter system-wide time.

item.title: 20. Learning Jazz Pianist Style with Cross-Attention Conditioning
item.description:
42 points by ishan0102 on 2026-10-05T22:30:52

This project asks whether a generative model can imitate jazz piano style the way Dick Hyman did in his 1994 book *In the Styles of… The Great Jazz Pianists* — composing new music in a master's manner rather than transcribing solos. The researchers fine-tune Aria, a transformer pretrained on piano MIDI, on solo performances of twelve jazz pianists from the PiJAMA dataset (including Tatum, Garner, Peterson, and Hyman himself), adding gated cross-attention blocks that read a learned pianist embedding in each of the last eight layers, with a gate initialized at 0.1. Because the embedding is attended to at every generation step, conditioning persists rather than fading like a prompt prefix. Evaluation shows that perplexity is nearly blind to style (6.82 vs. 6.96 for the unconditioned fine-tuned model), but a pianist classifier sliding along generated continuations names the intended pianist 70% of the time, versus 37% without conditioning and 25% for pretrained Aria. A classifier trained only on generated music then identifies real recordings with 87% accuracy on short chunks and 95% on full songs, within nine points of one trained on real data; turned on real performances, it also highlights where a pianist's style is most concentrated. Results vary by artist — Hank Jones and Dick Hyman reach 96% attribution, Cedar Walton only 29% — and the twelve pianists were chosen because PiJAMA recordings are already most separable to a pretrained model. The interactive demos generate twelve takes of the same opening of "Ain't Misbehavin'" from a single prompt, plus best-of-eight continuations from each pianist's own playing, rendered as MIDI in the browser, with a blindfold guessing game; all audio is generated, and shown takes are selected samples checked against the training corpus for non-memorization. The work, presented at ISMIR 2026 by Drew Edwards, Akira Maezawa, and Simon Dixon, acknowledges that scores come from a classifier rather than listeners — with its own biases, notably favoring Hyman — and flags a human listening study as the natural next step. Code, checkpoints, and evaluation scripts are on GitHub.

item.title: 22. The Future of Mathematics
item.description:
111 points by smilelamp on 2026-10-05T19:22:40

Jeremy Avigad reflects on how recent AI developments — particularly foundation models and agentic systems like Lean FRO's Lean theorem prover — are disrupting mathematics' traditional workflow, in which results respectable a year ago can now be generated by AI. While recognizing that day-to-day practice will change, he argues mathematics as a culture of rigorous reasoning remains indispensable and points to historical precedents for how new tools (algebraic methods, infinitesimals, set theory, symbolic computation) were once disconcerting but eventually absorbed. He proposes three responses for mathematicians: pursue genuinely harder problems, since current models excel at cobbling together existing techniques rather than originating the kind of field-transforming insights exemplified by Riemann's 1853 lecture on the foundations of geometry; "think bigger thoughts," since mathematicians choose their own problems and questions, and no reinforcement-learning setup could have evaluated Riemann's decisions whose value unfolds over long time horizons; and "try new things," treating work on proof assistants and neural networks as mathematics proper rather than mere technical labor. Mathematics departments, leaders, and journals are holding emergency meetings, and Avigad's message to early-career researchers is that the community stands with them, that mathematics remains as important as ever, and that the coming years will be extremely interesting — a remark cut off in the source text.

item.title: 25. Mosquitoes Are a Choice
item.description:
25 points by abe94 on 2026-10-05T14:49:09

Mosquito-borne diseases are returning to the United States as temperatures rise and insects develop pesticide resistance: 2024 saw nearly 4,000 dengue cases (a 360% jump over the prior decade's average), with local transmission in Florida, California, Texas and a public health emergency in Puerto Rico, plus the country's first locally acquired malaria cases in twenty years in 2023. Two genetic techniques could eliminate the threat domestically — a gene-edited male mosquito whose daughters die before adulthood (Oxitec's technology, which cut Aedes aegypti populations by 80% in the Cayman Islands and about 95% in Brazil) and Wolbachia-infected mosquitoes, which make carriers less able to transmit viruses and can function as sterile males — and Wolbachia cuts dengue infections by roughly 70% in Singapore trials, with full EPA registration granted in April 2024. The obstacle has been regulation rather than science: Oxitec's 2010 application was bounced between the USDA, FDA (which treats altered genomic DNA in animals as a "drug") and EPA, field trials in the Florida Keys and California were paused amid public opposition, the permit expired in April 2024, and full commercial registration remains pending after a scientific advisory panel review was postponed. The piece argues the US — sufficiently well-resourced and its disease-carrying mosquito population sufficiently small — could stamp out these diseases within its borders, but the 1986 Coordinated Framework, the last major biotech regulation, still governs jurisdictions poorly fitted to new technologies, and agencies are under-resourced; no new biotech regulation has been passed in decades, even as capabilities like DNA editing and engineered bacteria have advanced enormously.
